a: On "A Silent Dove Far Away."
t: A tune name nobody can explain
p: Yonat elem rechoqim is probably the name of a tune. The words are 'dove', 'silence' (or 'terebinths') and 'far off'.
b: The Hebrew 'al yonat elem rechoqim stands where other titles name a tune or setting, so most scholars take it as the first words of a known song. Yonat is "dove of". Elem as pointed means "silence"; with other vowels it is elim, "terebinth trees" or "gods". Rechoqim is "far away" or "distant ones". So the tune may be "The Dove of the Distant Terebinths" or "A Silent Dove Far Away". The Greek translators read it as a description instead: "for the people who have been removed far from the holy things", and many Jewish and Christian readers heard David, an exile among the Philistines, as the far-off dove (compare 55:6).
orig: עַל־יוֹנַת אֵלֶם רְחֹקִים ('al yonat elem rechoqim)

a: A miktam of David
t: Miktam, and how the titles are numbered
p: Psalms 56 to 60 are five miktams. The word is unexplained; the Greek calls each an inscription on a stone pillar.
b: Miktam appears only in the titles of Psalm 16 and Psalms 56 to 60. Proposals include "a golden poem" (from ketem, gold), "an inscription", or "a psalm of atonement". The Greek translates it stēlographia, "writing on a stele", as if these prayers were meant to be carved and kept. The site keeps the word as it is (see 16:0). One more thing to know before reading this part: Hebrew Bibles count a psalm's title as verse 1, so their verse numbers here run one higher than English ones (two higher in Psalm 60, whose long title fills two Hebrew verses), except in Psalms 66 and 72, whose short titles share verse 1 with the first line, and Psalm 71, which has no title. The site uses the English numbers, with titles as verse 0.

a: when the Philistines seized him in Gath
p: The title points to 1 Samuel 21, when David fled to Achish of Gath and pretended to be mad.
b: In 1 Samuel 21:10–15 David runs from Saul to Gath, a Philistine city. Achish's servants recognize him as the hero of the song about "his tens of thousands", and David "was badly frightened of Achish king of Gath" (1 Samuel 21:12). The narrative does not say he was arrested, only that he played the madman "in their grip" (1 Samuel 21:13), which may be what "seized" refers to. Psalm 34 is also tied to this episode, though its title names the king Abimelech. The psalm's fear, its watched heels and twisted words fit a man living among enemies who know who he is.

a: a man tramples me down
p: Sha'af can mean 'pant after' or 'trample, crush'. Either way the enemy is pressing in.
b: The verb sha'af appears in 56:1 and 56:2 and again in 57:3. It can mean to gasp or pant (Job 7:2, a slave longing for shade) or to snap at, trample or crush (Amos 2:7). Older English took it as "swallow up" (KJV). Here the parallel line, "he fights me and squeezes me hard", favors the image of being stamped on. The singular "man" (enosh, mortal man) becomes "my enemies" in the next line: one class of person, many people.

a: O Most High
p: Marom, 'height', can be God's title, or describe the enemies: 'from on high', 'proudly'.
b: The last word of the verse is marom, "height". The KJV and Jerome took it as a title addressed to God, "O thou most High", and the site follows that because the psalm is a prayer and marom is used of God in 92:8. The Greek has "from the height", and many modern versions take it as "proudly" or "from their high places": the enemies attack from a position of power. Both are possible and the Hebrew cannot decide.

a: In God I praise his word.
p: 56:4 and 56:10–11 repeat as a refrain, the second time with the name LORD added.
b: The psalm is built around a refrain: "In God I praise his word. In God I have trusted, and I do not fear." It returns in 56:10–11 with an extra line naming the LORD. Each time it follows a section of complaint (56:1–3, 56:5–9). Which "word" is praised is not said: a promise God has given, perhaps through a priest or prophet, that the singer holds onto. The question of the second refrain returns in 118:6 almost word for word: "What can a human being do to me?" (118:6), and from there in Hebrews 13:6.

a: What will flesh do to me?
p: Basar, 'flesh', means human beings as frail and mortal, set against God.
b: Basar here is not the body as opposed to the soul. It is humanity as weak and passing, the way Isaiah 31:3 says Egypt's horses are "flesh and not spirit" and Isaiah 40:6 says "all flesh is grass". The second refrain says the same with "a human being" (adam, 56:11). The contrast is between God and anyone who is not God. Paul's later use of "flesh" for sinful human nature grows out of this sense but is not what the psalm means.

a: They watch my heels
p: To watch someone's heels is to follow close behind, tracking every step.
b: The enemies "guard" or "watch" (shamar) the singer's heels, meaning they shadow his steps looking for a chance to strike. The same picture appears in Psalm 49:5 and in enemies who "set an ambush" (59:3). The Ketiv (the written text) and the Qere (the reading the scribes marked to be said aloud) differ slightly in the verb "they lie hidden", but both mean an ambush.

a: Store my tears in your wineskin.
p: God is asked to keep the singer's tears in a skin bottle, as something precious and counted.
b: A nod is a leather bag for water, milk or wine (Joshua 9:4; Judges 4:19). The singer asks God to collect every tear in one, so that none is lost or forgotten. The next line moves to a written record: "Are they not in your scroll?" The wordplay is strong in Hebrew: nodi "my wandering" and nodekha "your bottle" sound almost the same. The popular idea that ancient mourners kept "tear bottles" (lachrymatories) comes from later small glass bottles found in tombs; archaeologists now think most held perfume, so the psalm is better read as a picture than as a custom.

a: Are they not in your scroll?
p: The psalms picture God keeping written records of his people's lives, sorrows and names.
b: God's "scroll" or "book" appears often: Moses asks to be blotted out of it (Exodus 32:32), the singer of 139:16 says all his days were written there, Malachi 3:16 speaks of a scroll of remembrance, and Psalm 69:28 asks that the wicked be wiped out of the scroll of life. Here the scroll records tears, so suffering is not lost from God's memory. The image grew into the books opened at the judgment in Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 20:12.

a: God is on my side
p: The Hebrew is just three words: 'God (is) to me'.
b: Ki elohim li is compact: "that God is mine" or "that God is for me". It is the confidence Paul echoes in Romans 8:31 ("If God is for us, who is against us?"), though Paul quotes no psalm there. Psalm 118:6 makes the same point with the divine name: "With the LORD for me, I have no fear" (118:6).

a: In the LORD I praise a word.
t: God and the LORD: the Elohistic Psalter
p: Psalms 42–83 prefer the word 'God' (Elohim) to the name YHWH. Here the name slips back in.
b: Across Psalms 42 to 83 the general word Elohim ("God") is used about four times as often as the name YHWH ("the LORD"), the reverse of the rest of the Psalter. Scholars call this group the Elohistic Psalter. The clearest proof that an editor changed the name is that duplicate psalms differ: Psalm 53 has "God" where Psalm 14 has "the LORD", and Psalm 70 does the same with Psalm 40 (see 70:1). Why it was done is unknown: reverence for the name, or the habit of one collection. Here the refrain adds a line with the LORD, perhaps because the editor left it untouched. The Hebrew of 56:10 also says simply "a word" (davar), where 56:4 has "his word" (devaro).

a: The vows I made to you are on me
t: Vows paid with a thank offering
p: People in danger made vows to God and paid them afterward with a sacrifice at the sanctuary.
b: Someone in trouble might promise a gift to God if rescued (Genesis 28:20–22; 1 Samuel 1:11). Once rescued, the person came to the sanctuary to "pay" the vow, often with a todah, a thank offering, eaten in a meal with family and friends (Leviticus 7:11–16). Laments that end with a vow, like this one, may have been sung when the vow was made or at the meal when it was paid. Psalm 66:13–15 shows the paying.

a: in the light of life
t: The light of life, or of the living
p: Chayyim can mean 'life' or 'the living'. Either way, it is the opposite of the darkness of death.
b: To "walk before God in the light of life" is to live on in his presence, in the sunlit world of the living, instead of going down to the dark of the dead. The same words close Job 33:30. Psalm 116:9 repeats much of this verse: "I will walk about in the LORD's presence / in the lands of the living" (116:9). Jesus' saying that his followers will have "the light of life" (John 8:12) uses the same phrase.

a: On "Do Not Destroy."
p: Al tashcheth heads Psalms 57, 58, 59 and 75. It is probably a tune name.
b: Al tashcheth means "Do not destroy". It may be the first words of a well-known song; Isaiah 65:8 quotes a vintage saying, "Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it." Others connect it with David's words to Abishai when Saul lay asleep, "Do not destroy him" (1 Samuel 26:9), or with Moses' plea in Deuteronomy 9:26. The Greek translated the words, "Do not destroy", without saying what they mean.

a: when he ran away from Saul into the cave
p: David hid in the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22) and later in a cave near En-gedi, where Saul came in (1 Samuel 24).
b: Two caves figure in David's flight from Saul. After Gath he "fled to the cave of Adullam" (1 Samuel 22:1). Later, in the wilds of En-gedi, Saul went into a cave to relieve himself while "deep in the back of the cave sat David and his men" (1 Samuel 24:3). Psalm 142's title also mentions the cave. Readers who link this psalm to En-gedi note the title tune "Do Not Destroy" and David's refusal to harm Saul. Most critical scholars treat the title as a later reader's link to a fitting story.

a: In the shadow of your wings I shelter
p: The wings may be a mother bird's, or the cherubim's wings over the ark in the temple.
b: The phrase appears in 17:8, 36:7, 57:1, 61:4, 63:7 and 91:4. Some hear a mother bird sheltering her young (Deuteronomy 32:11; Matthew 23:37). Others think of the cherubim whose wings stretched over the ark in the inner room of the temple (1 Kings 8:6–7), so that to shelter under God's wings is to take refuge at his sanctuary, as fugitives did (1 Kings 1:50). Boaz blesses Ruth by "the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come for refuge" (Ruth 2:12). The two pictures may blend.

a: to the God who finishes his work for me
p: Gomer 'alay: 'who brings to an end for me', that is, who carries through what he has begun.
b: Gomer means to finish or bring to completion. The Hebrew has no object, so readers supply one: "who completes his purpose for me" (compare 138:8, "The LORD will complete it for me", with a related verb). The Greek reads "who has done good to me", perhaps from a different word (gomel, "deal fully with", as in 13:6). Either way the singer trusts God to finish the rescue.

a: God will send his loyal love and his faithfulness.
p: Hesed and emet are pictured as two servants God sends from heaven.
b: Hesed ("loyal love", the love that keeps faith within a bond) and emet ("faithfulness", reliability) are often paired (Exodus 34:6). Here they are almost persons, sent down like messengers to rescue the singer, as the same pair are asked to "guard" the king in 61:7 and "go before" God in 89:14. In 57:10 they reach to the heavens and clouds.

a: Rise up high over the heavens, God!
t: A refrain that turns the psalm
p: The same cry closes both halves of the psalm (57:5 and 57:11).
b: Psalm 57 falls into two halves, each closed by this refrain. The first half is a cry for help among "lions"; the second is a song of praise ready at dawn. The refrain asks God to show himself as king above the sky and over every land, so that his glory is seen everywhere. The prayer is not only for one man's rescue: when God saves the singer, his glory is shown to the nations (57:9).

a: they have fallen into the middle of it
t: The hunter caught in his own trap
p: A favorite theme of the Psalms: evil turns back on the one who plans it.
b: The enemies dig a pit for the singer and fall into it themselves. The same picture appears in 7:15, 9:15, 35:7–8 and Proverbs 26:27 ("The one who digs a pit falls into it"). The psalms often ask God to act this way, not by a bolt from heaven but by letting evil plans backfire. Esther, where Haman hangs on his own pole, is a whole story built on it.

a: My heart is firm, God; my heart is firm.
p: 57:7–11 is reused almost word for word as 108:1–5, joined to 60:5–12.
b: Psalm 108 is made of two pieces of this part of the Psalter: 57:7–11 followed by 60:5–12. The joined psalm drops the laments that opened both originals and keeps only the confident praise and the promise. Small differences show the editing: 108 has "the LORD" in 108:3 where 57:9 has "Lord", and 108:1 adds "also my glory". The reuse shows that the psalms were not frozen texts but songs that worshipers could combine for new needs. See the notes at 108:1.

a: Wake up, my glory!
p: Kavod, 'glory, honor', may here mean the self. Some revocalize it kaved, 'liver', the seat of feeling.
b: The singer tells his kavod to wake up. In 7:5, 16:9 and 30:12 kavod stands in parallel with "soul" or "heart", so it seems to mean the singer's inner self, his whole dignified being. Some scholars read kaved, "liver", which in Hebrew and Akkadian poetry can be the seat of emotion, just as English uses "heart". The Greek reads "my glory".

a: I will wake the dawn.
p: Instead of the dawn waking him, the singer will wake the dawn with music.
b: Ancient poetry personified the dawn (Job 3:9; Psalm 139:9). The bold boast is that the singer, rescued, will be up before morning and his harp and lyre (nevel and kinnor, two stringed instruments) will rouse the day. Rabbinic tradition used this verse for David himself: the Talmud (Berakhot 3b) tells that a lyre hung over David's bed and the north wind played it at midnight, waking him to study and pray until dawn.

a: You gods, do you truly speak justice?
p: Rulers and judges, or heavenly beings who rule the nations? The same question arises in Psalm 82.
b: If the word is elim, "gods" (see the variant), the psalm addresses beings who are supposed to judge human beings fairly and do not. Many interpreters think of human rulers and judges, who were sometimes called "gods" because they judged in God's place (compare Exodus 21:6; 22:8, where ha'elohim may mean the judges at the sanctuary). Others, comparing Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32:8, think of the divine council, the heavenly powers God set over the nations, who have failed in their task. In either case the charge is the same: those meant to do justice are doing violence.

a: The wicked turn aside from the womb.
p: A poetic exaggeration of how deep the evil runs, not a doctrine of birth.
b: The psalm says the wicked have gone wrong "from the womb" and liars "from the belly". In the context of a curse on unjust rulers, most commentators read this as rhetoric: their lying is as old as they are, part of their nature. Christian theologians (Augustine, Calvin) cited it with 51:5 as support for original sin, the teaching that all people are born with a bent toward sin. Others note that the psalm divides the wicked from the righteous, rather than saying all are wicked. See the discussion of 51:5 in its own part.

a: like a deaf cobra that stops up its ear
p: Snake charmers worked in Egypt and the Near East for thousands of years. A deaf cobra cannot be charmed.
b: The peten is probably the Egyptian cobra. Charmers (melachashim, "whisperers") were known in Egypt and Mesopotamia, and Jeremiah 8:17 and Ecclesiastes 10:11 mention them. Snakes cannot actually hear airborne sound well, and respond to the charmer's movement, but the ancient belief was that the spell worked through the ear. A snake that "stops up its ear" is the worst kind: no word can tame it. So it is with rulers who will not listen.

a: God, smash their teeth in their mouths!
t: How to read a curse psalm
p: Psalm 58 is one of the harshest prayers in the Bible. It asks God, not the singer, to break the wicked.
b: Verses 6–10 pile up wishes: broken fangs, water draining away, blunted arrows, a dissolving snail, a stillborn child, the righteous washing their feet in blood. Several things help a modern reader. The targets are unjust rulers (58:1–2), not personal rivals. The violence is handed over to God; the singer does nothing himself. The goal is that people will say "a God exists who judges on the earth" (58:11). Even so, the Roman Catholic Liturgy of the Hours leaves Psalm 58 out of its four-week cycle. See the chapter page and the topic page.

a: let his arrows be as if cut off
p: The Hebrew is very hard: 'let him tread (bend) his arrows, like they are cut off'.
b: Word for word the line says "let him bend his arrows, as if they are cut off". Who "he" is is unclear: God aiming at the wicked, or the wicked aiming at the innocent. The rendering here takes it as a wish that the enemy's arrows be headless and harmless. The Greek has "He will bend his bow until they grow weak". The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has "his arrow", the spoken reading (Qere) "his arrows".
orig: יִדְרֹךְ חִצָּיו כְּמוֹ יִתְמֹלָלוּ (yidrokh chitsav kemo yitmolalu)

a: like a snail that dissolves as it goes
p: People thought a snail wore itself away in its own slime as it moved.
b: Shablul is probably a snail or slug. The trail of slime it leaves looked as if the creature were melting away as it crawled, and in the dry season snails shrivel in their shells. The point is that the wicked should vanish as a snail seems to. The next picture, a stillborn child, is even starker: something that never lived to see the light.

a: Before your pots can feel the thorn fire
p: A cooking picture: the storm sweeps the fire away before the pot even warms.
b: Thorns made a quick, hot fire for cooking (Ecclesiastes 7:6). The verse seems to say that before the pots feel the heat of the burning thorns, whether still green or already alight, God will sweep it all away in a storm. So sudden will the end of the wicked be. Every word is uncertain: sir can be "pot" or "thorn", chay "green, raw" or "living", and charon "burning" or "anger" (the KJV has "both living, and in his wrath"). Commentators admit the text may be damaged.
orig: בְּטֶרֶם יָבִינוּ סִּירֹתֵיכֶם אָטָד (beterem yavinu sirotekhem atad)

a: He will wash his feet in the wicked one's blood.
p: A battlefield image of total victory, also found in 68:23 and in Canaanite poetry.
b: Victors walking through a battlefield waded in blood. The image appears again in 68:23, and the Ugaritic goddess Anat is said to wade knee-deep in the blood of warriors (KTU 1.3 ii). The psalm uses the stock picture to say that the wicked will be utterly defeated and the righteous vindicated. The Greek and the Latin (Gallican Psalter) have "his hands" instead of "his feet", and Augustine worked from that text. Many Christian readers, following Augustine, read it spiritually: the righteous are made clean by seeing God's judgment on sin. The Jewish and Christian traditions alike have found this verse hard to pray as it stands.

a: Yes, a God exists who judges on the earth.
p: The verb 'judges' is plural in Hebrew, which may mean 'gods' or simply God's majesty.
b: Elohim shofetim ba'arets: elohim is plural in form but means "God" with a singular verb almost everywhere. Here the participle shofetim is plural too, as in a few other places where God is the subject (Genesis 20:13; 2 Samuel 7:23). Some read it as a quiet answer to 58:1: the "gods" do not judge rightly, but God does. The psalm ends where it began, with justice on the earth. Fruit for the righteous means a real reward, the result of a life.

a: when Saul sent men, and they watched the house in order to kill him
p: The title points to 1 Samuel 19:11–17, when Michal let David down through a window.
b: "Saul sent messengers to David's house to keep watch on him and kill him in the morning" (1 Samuel 19:11). Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, warned him and let him down through a window. The psalm's men who "come back at evening" and "go around the city" like dogs (59:6, 14) fit a night watch on a house. But the psalm also speaks of "all the nations" (59:5, 8) and God ruling "in Jacob to the ends of the earth" (59:13), which suggests a king or the people of Israel facing foreign enemies. Many scholars think a national prayer was later linked to the story of David.

a: Lift me high above those who rise against me
p: Sagav, 'set high', means to put someone out of reach, as on a high wall or crag.
b: Tesaggeveni is from the same root as misgav, "high fortress", the word for God in 59:9, 59:16 and 59:17. The singer asks to be lifted to a place enemies cannot reach, and then names God as that place. The same image appears in 20:1, 69:29 and 91:14.

a: not for any crime of mine, and not for my sin, LORD
p: The singer claims to be innocent in this conflict, not perfect in all things.
b: Pesha' ("crime, rebellion") and chatta't ("sin") are two of the main Hebrew words for wrongdoing. The protest that the attack is "not for any crime of mine" belongs to the language of the courtroom: in this case, the accused is innocent (compare 7:3–5; 17:3–5). It does not claim a sinless life. Psalm 69 shows the balance: the singer is hated "without a cause" (69:4), yet admits "God, you know my foolishness" (69:5).

a: Wake up to meet me, and see!
p: The psalms boldly tell God to wake up, though they also say he never sleeps.
b: Calls for God to "wake up" or "rouse yourself" appear in 7:6, 35:23, 44:23 and here (59:4–5). Psalm 121:4 insists that Israel's guardian never sleeps. The prayers are not making a claim about God's nature but describing how things feel to someone waiting for help. In Canaanite myth Baal really did sleep and need waking (compare Elijah's taunt, 1 Kings 18:27); Israel's poets borrow the language but never the idea of a weak god.

a: LORD God of Armies, God of Israel
p: A piled-up title: the name YHWH, 'God', 'of Armies' and 'God of Israel'.
b: The Hebrew stacks titles: YHWH elohim tseva'ot elohei yisra'el. "The LORD of Armies" (tseva'ot, hosts) is the site's rendering throughout: the armies may be Israel's, the angels, or the stars. The unusual combination "LORD God of Armies" occurs also in 80:4, 80:19 and 84:8, all in the Elohistic Psalter, and some think "God" (elohim) was added beside the name by the same editor who changed many YHWHs to Elohim (see 56:10).

a: wake up to punish all the nations
p: The psalm moves from personal enemies to all the nations. Who is the singer?
b: If David's house is under watch (59:0), why ask God to punish "all the nations"? Readers answer in three ways. Some say David speaks of Saul's men as no better than godless foreigners. Many scholars think a king or leader prays when Jerusalem is surrounded by foreign armies, perhaps in the time of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18–19), and the psalm was linked to David later. Others think it began as one person's prayer and was widened for use by the community. The repeated "they come back at evening" may then picture enemy scouts prowling outside the city walls.

a: They growl like dogs
p: In Israel dogs were scavengers that roamed streets and dumps at night, not pets.
b: Most dogs in ancient Israel were half-wild scavengers that lived off garbage and carcasses (1 Kings 14:11; 21:23–24). They prowled the streets after dark, snarling and hungry. To call someone a dog was an insult (1 Samuel 17:43; 24:14; 2 Samuel 9:8). The enemies "come back at evening" each night, like a pack circling the town. The same image surrounds the sufferer in 22:16 and 22:20.

a: "For who is listening?"
p: The enemies think no one hears them, not even God.
b: The enemies speak with "swords on their lips" and say, "Who is listening?" It is the boast of the practical atheist: God either does not exist or does not care (10:4; 10:11; 14:1; 64:5; 94:7). The next verse is God's answer: he laughs at them (59:8), as he laughs at the rebel kings in 2:4.

a: My Strength, I will watch for you
p: The singer will keep watch for God, as the enemies keep watch on his house.
b: There is a play on watching. Saul's men "watched" the house (59:0, shamar); the singer will "watch" (eshmorah) for God, keeping a lookout for his help like a watchman on the wall. Psalm 59 has a refrain at 59:9 and 59:17, which the singer changes: "I will watch for you" becomes "I will make music to you" (azammerah), the same letters almost but with praise in place of waiting.

a: Do not kill them, or my people may forget.
t: Do not kill them ... finish them
p: The psalm asks God not to kill the enemies quickly (59:11), then to finish them (59:13).
b: The two requests seem to clash. The best reading is that the singer wants a slow, public fall: if the enemies vanished at once, people would soon forget what God had done. Let them stagger and wander, as a living lesson, before they are ended. Augustine read 59:11 in a very different way that had a long history: he took it as God's command not to kill the Jews, who should be scattered but kept alive as witnesses to the Scriptures (City of God 18.46). This "witness" teaching protected Jews in some medieval law but also justified their humiliation. Most Christians today reject the reading.

a: The sin of their mouth is the word of their lips.
p: As in many laments, the enemies' main weapon is speech: lies, curses, slander.
b: Psalm 59 says the enemies' mouths spill out words like swords (59:7) and that every word they say is sin. Their weapons are cursing and lying (59:12). In the ancient world a curse was not only rude but thought to have power to harm (Numbers 22:6). The prayer asks that they be "caught in their pride", trapped by the very words they speak.

a: If they are not filled, they stay all night.
p: Vayalinu can mean 'they stay the night' or 'they growl, grumble'. The Greek has 'they will grumble'.
b: The form vayalinu can come from lun, "spend the night", or from the related root "grumble, murmur" (used of Israel in the wilderness, Exodus 16:2). The Greek and the KJV ("grudge") take it as "growl". The site follows the more common sense: if the dogs do not find enough, they stay out all night hunting. The contrast is with the singer, who will "in the morning" shout for joy (59:16).

a: In the morning I will shout for joy at your loyal love
p: The dogs prowl at night; God's loyal love comes in the morning.
b: The psalm sets the night of danger against the morning of rescue. Help at daybreak is a common theme (46:5; 30:5; 90:14; 143:8): it may reflect the custom of hearing cases and giving verdicts in the morning, the time when God's help was expected at the sanctuary, or simply the end of a frightening night. Christians later sang this verse at morning prayer.

a: On "Lily of the Testimony."
p: Probably another tune name: 'the lily of the testimony' or 'the lily is a decree'.
b: Shushan eduth appears only here; compare shoshannim eduth in 80:0 and "Lilies" in 45:0 and 69:0. Eduth means a testimony, a solemn decree or covenant document (the tablets of the law are "the testimony", Exodus 25:16). Some think of a lily-shaped instrument or an oracle given by lot. The Greek has "for those who will yet be changed", reading the words in an entirely different way.

a: for teaching
p: Lelammed: this psalm was meant to be taught, perhaps learned by heart.
b: Only this title says a psalm is "for teaching". Compare David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, which he ordered to be taught to the people of Judah (2 Samuel 1:18), and the Song of Moses, written down to teach Israel (Deuteronomy 31:19). A song of defeat and recovered hope was a lesson worth passing on.

a: Joab came back and struck down twelve thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt
p: 2 Samuel 8:13 gives eighteen thousand and names David; 1 Chronicles 18:12 credits Abishai.
b: The title links the psalm with David's wars against the Aramean kingdoms of Zobah and "Aram of the two rivers" (Aram-naharaim, northern Mesopotamia) and with Edom (2 Samuel 8:3–14; 10:6–19). The numbers and names differ across the accounts: 2 Samuel 8:13 says David "struck down eighteen thousand men of Edom in the Valley of Salt"; 1 Chronicles 18:12 says "Abshai son of Zeruiah struck Edom in the Valley of Salt: eighteen thousand men"; this title gives Joab and twelve thousand. Different sources, or different stages of one campaign, may lie behind them. The Valley of Salt is probably south of the Dead Sea.

a: You have thrown us off, God.
p: The title celebrates victory, but the psalm opens with defeat. Why?
b: The body of the psalm laments that God has rejected his people and no longer goes out with their armies (60:10). The title remembers David's victories. Readers who hold to the title imagine an Edomite raid on Judah while David's army was away in the north (compare 1 Kings 11:15–16), so that the psalm was prayed in the crisis before Joab's victory. Many scholars instead date it to a later defeat, often by Edom, such as the loss of the land after 587 BC (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7). The title then shows how later readers found hope in David's story.

a: wine to drink that makes us reel
p: God's anger is pictured as strong wine that makes those who drink it reel.
b: Yayin tar'elah, "wine of reeling", is the first appearance of an image the prophets use often: God hands a cup to a nation, and they drink and stagger as judgment (Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15–17; Habakkuk 2:16). In 75:8 the LORD holds the cup. Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, "take this cup from me", draws on the same picture (Mark 14:36).

a: for them to rally to, away from the bow
t: A banner: to flee to, or a sign of victory?
p: The verse can mean a rallying point out of bowshot, or (from Aramaic) a banner raised for the truth.
b: A nes is a pole with a flag or emblem, the point around which troops gather (Isaiah 11:12; Exodus 17:15). Lehitnoses may mean "to rally to" or "to be lifted up". Mipne qoshet may mean "away from the bow", that is, out of arrow range, or, taking qoshet as the Aramaic word for "truth", "because of the truth" (KJV). The Greek has "a sign, so that they might flee from the face of the bow". A bitter reading is also possible: God gave the banner only so that his people could gather to run away.
orig: נֵּס לְהִתְנוֹסֵס מִפְּנֵי קֹשֶׁט (nes lehitnoses mipne qoshet)

a: God spoke in his holiness:
p: 60:6–8 is a divine speech, perhaps given by a priest or prophet at the temple in answer to the lament.
b: "In his holiness" may mean "by his holy nature" (as in an oath, 89:35) or "in his sanctuary" (the Greek has "in his holy place"). Many scholars think laments like this one were answered by a word from God spoken through a temple prophet or priest, and that 60:6–8 preserves one such answer. In it God speaks as a warrior dividing up his land: he owns the tribes west and east of the Jordan and treats the neighboring nations as servants.

a: I will split up Shechem,
p: Shechem west of the Jordan, Succoth east of it: the whole land, divided as an owner pleases.
b: Shechem, in the hills of Ephraim, and Succoth, in the Jordan valley east of the river, were both places where Jacob settled when he came back from Aram (Genesis 33:17–18). To divide them up and measure them out is what a conqueror or landowner does with his property (Joshua 18:10). God claims both sides of the Jordan as his.

a: Judah is my ruler's staff.
p: The northern tribe Ephraim is God's helmet, Judah his ruler's staff.
b: God arms himself with his tribes. Ephraim, the strongest northern tribe, is his helmet (literally "the protection of my head"). Judah, the royal tribe of David, is his mechoqeq, a ruler's staff or lawgiver's rod, as in Jacob's blessing: "The scepter will not leave Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet" (Genesis 49:10). The verse imagines the twelve tribes united under God, which suits David's reign.

a: On Edom I throw my sandal.
p: God treats Moab as a servant's basin and throws his sandal on Edom, a sign of ownership or contempt.
b: Returning warriors washed their feet; Moab will be the basin. Throwing a sandal onto land may be a legal act of claiming it (compare the sandal in Ruth 4:7 and Deuteronomy 25:9) or simply tossing one's shoes to a slave. Philistia is told to shout, either in fear or in forced homage; Psalm 108:9 has "over Philistia I shout", and the Greek here has "foreigners have been made subject". The Greek also has "Moab, the cauldron of my hope", reading the Hebrew differently.

a: Who will bring me into the fortified city?
p: Probably Bozrah or Sela, Edom's mountain strongholds.
b: Edom's capital Bozrah (Isaiah 34:6; 63:1) and the rock fortress Sela (2 Kings 14:7; Obadiah 3) sat high in the mountains south-east of the Dead Sea, hard for any army to take. The speaker, perhaps the king, asks who will lead him there. The answer is the next verse: only God, who seems to have abandoned the army.

a: With God we will do mighty things
p: Na'aseh chayil: literally 'we will do strength', that is, fight bravely and win.
b: Chayil is strength, valor, wealth or an army. To "do chayil" is to act with strength (Numbers 24:18, where Edom too is the target: "while Israel does mighty deeds"). The psalm ends where it should: the help of human beings is empty (60:11), but with God the army can win. The same ending closes Psalm 108.

a: I call to you from the edge of the earth
t: From the end of the earth
p: Exile, a far-off battle, or the edge of death? 'The end of the earth' may be literal or a figure.
b: Miqtseh ha'arets is "from the end of the earth". Some take it literally: the singer is far from Jerusalem, perhaps an exile or a king at war, longing for the temple (61:4). Others take it as the edge of the world of the living, close to the underworld, like the depths of 69:2 and 71:20. Jewish tradition heard the voice of Israel scattered among the nations. Calvin and Augustine both read it as the whole church praying from every land.

a: Lead me onto a rock that is too high for me.
p: A place the singer cannot climb alone. God must lead him there.
b: The Hebrew says "a rock that is higher than I" or "too high for me". The singer cannot reach safety by his own strength; God must lead him up, as a guide leads a climber. Rock as refuge runs through these psalms (62:2, 62:6–7; 71:3). The hymn "Lead me to the Rock" and Christian readings that see Christ as the rock (1 Corinthians 10:4) draw on this verse.

a: Let me be a guest in your tent forever.
p: Gur is to live as a guest or resident foreigner under someone's protection.
b: Agurah is from gur, the verb behind ger, "a foreigner who lives among you". The singer asks to live under God's protection in his "tent", the old word for the sanctuary from the days of the tabernacle (15:1; 27:5–6). A guest in the ancient Near East was under the host's care and could not be harmed. See also 15:1 and 23:6.

a: the possession of those who fear your name
p: Yerushat, 'inheritance, possession', is strange here; many scholars read 'the desire' of those who fear God.
b: The Hebrew yerushat yir'ei shemekha is "the possession (inheritance) of those who fear your name": perhaps the land, or a share among God's people. The Greek agrees (klēronomian, "inheritance"). Because the word is unusual after "you have listened to my vows", many scholars emend to areshet, "the request" or "desire" (as in 21:2): "you have granted the desire of those who fear your name". The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: Add days to the king's days
p: The psalm suddenly speaks of the king in the third person. Is the singer the king himself?
b: 61:6–7 prays for long life for the king, "generation after generation", and that he sit enthroned before God forever. If the singer is the king (as the title "Of David" suggests), he speaks of himself in the third person, as kings sometimes did. Others think the community or a priest adds a prayer for the king to an individual's prayer. The Targum reads "King Messiah" here (Hebrew 61:7), since no human king lives forever; Rashi reads it of David's own life. Christian readers took it of Christ, whose kingdom has no end.

a: Appoint loyal love and faithfulness to guard him.
p: Man, before the verb 'guard', may be 'appoint', 'who', or 'manna'. Its meaning is unknown.
b: The Hebrew has chesed ve'emet man yintseruhu: "loyal love and faithfulness, man, let them guard him". Man may be a short form of the verb manah, "appoint" (so most versions), the Aramaic word "who" ("who will guard him?"), or a scribal mistake. The Greek reads it as "who" (tis): "his mercy and truth, who will seek them out?", which is the strongest support for the second option. The sense is clear anyway: love and faithfulness are to stand guard over the king like two bodyguards (compare 57:3; 89:14).

a: On Jeduthun.
p: Jeduthun was one of David's three chief temple musicians, with Asaph and Heman.
b: 1 Chronicles 16:41–42 and 25:1–6 name Jeduthun (also called Ethan) as a leader of the Levite singers, with his sons playing lyres "to prophesy". Psalm 39 is "for Jeduthun", and Psalms 62 and 77 are "on" or "according to" Jeduthun. The preposition 'al here may mean a musical style named for him, or a guild of singers descended from him.

a: Yes, my soul is quiet before God.
p: Psalm 62 starts six lines with akh, a small word meaning 'only', 'surely' or 'yes'.
b: The particle akh begins 62:1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 9. It can limit ("only") or affirm ("surely, yes"). Read as "only", the psalm says that God alone is the singer's rock; read as "yes", it presses a point home again and again. The site uses "Yes" every time so that readers can see the repeated word; the sense "only God" is there too. Psalm 39, also tied to Jeduthun, uses akh in the same way (39:5–6, 11).

a: my soul is quiet
p: Dumiyyah is stillness, the quiet of someone who has stopped struggling and waits.
b: Dumiyyah, "silence", comes from the same family as the word in 65:1 and 37:7 ("Be still before the LORD"). It is not resignation but trust: the soul stops thrashing and rests in God. In 62:5 the singer speaks to his own soul, telling it to be quiet again. The Greek, reading the line as a question, has "Will not my soul be subject to God?"

a: as if he were a leaning wall, a fence pushed in
p: The victim is like a wall already tilting; one push and it falls.
b: The image is of a stone wall bulging outward, or a fence half pushed over, that needs only a shove to collapse. The enemies gang up on one man who already looks weak. Isaiah 30:13 uses the same picture for Judah's sin: "like a break in a high wall, bulging out, about to fall" (a fresh rendering; Isaiah is not yet on this site). Some take the wall as a picture of the enemies themselves, who will fall; the Hebrew allows both.

a: but in their inner parts they curse.
p: Flattery outside, cursing inside: a constant complaint in the psalms and wisdom books.
b: The enemies speak blessing and mean curse. Psalm 28:3 and 55:21 make the same complaint, and James 3:9–10 warns that "with it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse people" (a fresh rendering). In a world where curses were believed to have power, a smiling face that hid a curse was doubly dangerous.

a: With their mouth they bless,
p: The Hebrew has 'with his mouth': each of the enemies speaks one way and means another.
b: The Hebrew says befiv, "with his mouth", though the verbs around it are plural. The singular is distributive: each one of them blesses with his mouth. The Plain gives the sense with "their".

a: Pour out your hearts in front of him.
p: The singer turns to the congregation and teaches them what he has learned.
b: In 62:1–7 the singer speaks about God and to his own soul. In 62:8–12 he turns to "people" ('am, the gathered congregation) and teaches, like a wisdom teacher: trust God, not people or money. Pouring out the heart is the honest prayer of someone in distress, as Hannah said, "I have poured my soul out before the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:15). Psalm 62 is often classed as a psalm of trust with wisdom elements.

a: all together they weigh less than a breath
p: Hevel is the same word Ecclesiastes uses for 'meaningless' or 'a breath'.
b: Human beings, low and high, are hevel, a puff of breath, and on a merchant's scales they rise up because they weigh nothing. Hevel is the key word of Ecclesiastes ("Breath of breaths, all is breath") and also the name Abel. The two kinds of people are literally "sons of Adam" and "sons of a man" (bene adam and bene ish), which probably means common people and important people, as in 49:2.

a: If wealth bears fruit
t: Do not set your heart on riches
p: Wealth gained by force is worthless; even honest wealth must not hold the heart.
b: The verse moves from ill-gotten gain (extortion, robbery) to wealth in general. Even if riches "bear fruit" and grow, the heart must not lean on them. The same warning appears in 49:6–20, 52:7 and Job 31:24–25. Jesus' sayings about treasure and the heart (Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 12:15–21) and Paul's warning to the rich (1 Timothy 6:17) say much the same.

a: two times I heard this:
p: A numerical saying, 'one ... two', as in the wisdom books.
b: Hebrew poets liked numerical patterns: "The LORD hates six things, / and seven are abhorrent to his very self" (Proverbs 6:16), "For three crimes ... and for four" (Amos 1:3). Here God speaks once and the singer hears two things: that strength belongs to God, and that loyal love belongs to him. Jewish tradition (Talmud Sanhedrin 34a) used the verse to teach that one verse of Scripture can carry several meanings: "one thing God has spoken, two things I have heard."

a: for you pay each person back by what he does
t: Paid back for what one does
p: Quoted in substance in Matthew 16:27 and Romans 2:6, and in Proverbs 24:12.
b: This line is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements that God judges people by their deeds. The Greek has "according to his works", wording taken up in Romans 2:6, 2 Timothy 4:14 and Revelation 22:12, and Matthew 16:27 says the same in other words ("then he will pay back each one for the way he has acted"). Proverbs 24:12 says the same. The psalm sets it beside loyal love: God's justice and his love both belong to him.
r: Proverbs 24:12; Job 34:11; Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; 2 Timothy 4:14; Revelation 22:12

a: when he was in the wilderness of Judah
p: The dry hills between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, where David hid from Saul and fled from Absalom.
b: The wilderness of Judah is the barren land falling east from Jerusalem and Hebron down to the Dead Sea. David hid there from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14; 24:1) and crossed it when he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 15:23, 28; 17:29). Because 63:11 speaks of "the king", many who follow the title think of the flight from Absalom, when David was already king. The Greek of Rahlfs also has "Judea"; some Greek manuscripts have "Idumea".

a: I search hard for you
p: Shachar means 'seek eagerly', and sounds like shachar, 'dawn'. The Greek has 'I rise early to you'.
b: Ashachareka is from shachar, "to seek earnestly". The same letters spell shachar, "dawn", and the Greek translated "I rise at dawn to you" (orthrizō). That reading made Psalm 63 the church's great morning psalm: John Chrysostom (about AD 390) says the fathers appointed it to be sung every morning, and it still opens Lauds on Sundays in the Roman rite and is one of the six psalms of the Orthodox morning service (the Hexapsalmos).

a: in a dry and worn-out land without water
p: The desert's thirst is a picture of longing for God's presence.
b: The singer's soul and body both long for God the way a traveler in the Judean wilderness longs for water. The same image opens Psalm 42 ("As a deer longs for streams of water") and returns in 143:6. In John 4:13–14 and 7:37 Jesus offers living water to the thirsty, and Christian writers often read the psalm as the soul's thirst for Christ.

a: So I have looked at you in the holy place
p: The singer remembers seeing God's strength and glory in worship, perhaps in a festival.
b: "Seeing God" in the temple meant taking part in worship before the ark, where God's glory was present (27:4; 84:7). Some think the verse remembers a festival with the ark carried in procession (compare 68:24). The memory sustains the singer in the dry land. Whether he is far away or actually in the temple now is debated; the Hebrew tenses allow both.

a: Your loyal love is better than life itself
p: Hesed is worth more than life, so even death cannot cancel the reason to praise.
b: The claim is remarkable for a book that usually treats long life as God's great gift. If God's loyal love is better than life, then even the loss of life cannot take away what matters most. Christian martyrs and Jewish teachers alike quoted the verse. Rabbi Akiva's death with the Shema on his lips (Talmud Berakhot 61b), loving God "even if he takes your life", is a related thought.

a: I will raise my hands in your name.
p: Raising open hands was the ancient posture of prayer and blessing.
b: Israelites prayed standing, with hands lifted and palms turned up toward heaven (28:2; 134:2; 141:2; 1 Kings 8:22). Ancient Near Eastern art shows worshipers in the same pose. The early church kept it: the figures in Roman catacomb paintings pray with arms raised, and 1 Timothy 2:8 asks men to pray "lifting up holy hands". Many churches today, Pentecostal and charismatic above all, lift hands in worship.

a: As with fat and rich food my soul is filled
p: The richest food: the fat portions that belonged to God at the sacrifice.
b: Chelev vadeshen, "fat and fatness", is the richest food. In the sacrifices the fat belonged to God (Leviticus 3:16–17), so the image may come from the thanksgiving meal at the temple. To be "filled" with God is better than any feast. Isaiah 25:6 pictures the LORD's banquet for all peoples, "a feast of rich food".

a: Through the watches of the night I murmur about you.
p: The night was divided into three watches. Hagah is to murmur, to mutter over and over.
b: Israel divided the night into three "watches" (Judges 7:19; Lamentations 2:19). The singer lies awake through them. Hagah is the word used in 1:2 for "murmuring" God's law day and night: reading or reciting under one's breath. It can also be the growl of a lion (Isaiah 31:4) or the cooing of a dove (Isaiah 38:14). Prayer here is a low, steady murmur of remembrance.

a: My soul clings close behind you
p: Davaq achar: to stick close behind, the way Ruth clung to Naomi.
b: Davqah nafshi acharekha: "my soul clings behind you". Davaq is the verb for a man holding to his wife (Genesis 2:24), for Ruth clinging to Naomi (Ruth 1:14) and for Israel holding on to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20; 30:20). Here it adds "behind": the singer follows so close he cannot be shaken off, while God's right hand holds him up from the other side.

a: They will be a meal for jackals.
p: Shu'alim can be foxes or jackals. Jackals feed on corpses on a battlefield.
b: The word shu'al covered both foxes and jackals. Jackals, which hunt in packs and eat carrion, fit the picture of unburied bodies left after a battle; to lie unburied was the worst disgrace (Jeremiah 7:33). Samson's three hundred shu'alim in Judges 15:4 are also more likely jackals, which live in packs, than foxes.

a: Everyone who swears by him will boast
p: 'By him' may mean by God or by the king. Both were names used in oaths.
b: Israelites took oaths "by the life of the LORD" (1 Samuel 14:39) and sometimes also by the life of the king (1 Samuel 17:55; 2 Samuel 15:21). "Everyone who swears by him" may be the loyal worshipers of God (Deuteronomy 6:13) or the loyal subjects of the king. The verse joins the two: the king rejoices in God, and those loyal to God or king will be proud, while the liars, who swore falsely, are silenced.

a: They draw their arrow: a bitter word
p: Tongues are swords and words are arrows: the main weapons of the enemy in the psalms.
b: Psalm 64 is almost entirely about speech used as a weapon: sharpened tongues, words shot like arrows from ambush, secret plotting (64:2–6). Slander in an ancient village could destroy a family; in a court it could cost a life (1 Kings 21:10–13). The answer comes in 64:7: God has his own arrow, and the liars' tongues turn against them (64:8).

a: The inner self of a person, the heart, is deep.
p: The line may admire how cunning the plotters are, or say that only God sees the heart.
b: 64:6 is hard Hebrew. The first part seems to quote the plotters: tamnu chefes mechuppas, "we have completed a well-searched plan". Then comes the comment: "the inside of a man, and the heart, is deep." It may mean that human cunning runs very deep, so no one can see the plot coming. But "deep" things are exactly what God searches out (Jeremiah 17:9–10; Proverbs 20:27), so the line also prepares for God's sudden arrow.
orig: וְקֶרֶב אִישׁ וְלֵב עָמֹק (veqerev ish velev 'amoq)

a: But God shoots them with an arrow;
p: The same words come back on the enemies: they shot suddenly (64:4); God shoots suddenly.
b: The psalm is built on reversal. The enemies "shoot" (yarah) at the blameless "suddenly" (pit'om, 64:4); now God "shoots" them with an arrow and "suddenly" they are wounded. Their tongues, which were swords, make them stumble (64:8). The punishment fits the crime exactly, a pattern the Bible calls repaying in kind (Obadiah 15).

a: Their own tongue trips them up.
p: The Hebrew reads roughly 'they made him stumble, their tongue (is) upon them'.
b: The verb is plural with a singular object, and the second part has no verb: "and they made him stumble, upon them their tongue". The rendering here follows the likely sense, which most versions share: the enemies' own words bring them down. Those who see them "shake their heads" (yitnodedu), a gesture of scorn, or "run away" (KJV "flee away"), since the verb can mean either.

a: Then all people will be afraid.
p: God's judgment on the plotters becomes a lesson for everyone who sees it.
b: A private wrong, put right by God, becomes public teaching. "All people" (kol adam) fear, tell what God has done, and understand. The psalm moves from a hidden plot (64:2) to an open lesson, and ends with the righteous gladly taking refuge in the LORD (64:10), the pattern of many laments. Compare 52:6–7, where the righteous see God's judgment and learn from it.

a: For you, God, silence is praise in Zion
t: Silence, or a hymn that is fitting?
p: The Hebrew says 'silence is praise'; the Greek read a similar word, 'a hymn is fitting'.
b: Lekha dumiyyah tehillah: "to you, silence, praise". It may mean that silent awe is itself praise, or "praise waits in silence for you" (KJV "praise waiteth"), or, with different vowels (domiyyah, from damah, "be like, fit"), "praise is fitting for you", as the Greek has. Jewish teachers loved the Hebrew: Rashi and the Talmud (Megillah 18a) say that the best praise of God is silence, since no words are enough. See the variant.

a: all flesh will come to you
p: Zion's God hears prayer, so all humanity will come: an early hope for the nations.
b: "All flesh" is all humanity (Genesis 6:12; Isaiah 40:5). The psalm begins in Zion with Israel's vows and widens to the whole world: "all the ends of the earth" (65:5), "those who live at the far ends" (65:8). Solomon's prayer asked God to hear the foreigner who prays toward the temple (1 Kings 8:41–43), and Isaiah 56:7 calls it "a house of prayer for all peoples".

a: you make atonement for them
p: Kipper here has God as subject: he covers or wipes away the people's rebellions.
b: In Leviticus the priest "makes atonement" (kipper) by sacrifice. Here God himself does it, as in 78:38 and 79:9. Guilt that overpowers the singer ("Deeds of wrong have been too strong for me") is dealt with by God, and the result is welcome into his courts (65:4). The change from "me" to "our rebellions" joins the individual to the community.

a: Happy are those you choose and bring close
p: Ashrei is 'happy', 'fortunate', the word that opens the Psalter (1:1). Older English says 'blessed'.
b: Ashrei means "how fortunate, how happy". It describes a state of well-being, not a blessing spoken by someone else (that is barukh, "blessed"). The site translates it "Happy" throughout (see 1:1). Here the happy one is chosen and "brought close" (qarav, the word for bringing an offering near), to live in God's courts: perhaps a priest, a Levite, or any worshiper welcomed at the temple.

a: and the farthest sea
p: From Zion the view widens to the ends of the earth and the distant sea.
b: The psalm's world reaches from Zion to "the ends of the earth" and the far sea, the Mediterranean and beyond, where Tarshish lay (72:10). The God who answers Israel's prayers is the one in whom the farthest nations, knowingly or not, place their hope. Compare Isaiah 42:10: "you who go down to the sea" are called to sing a new song.

a: He calms the roar of the seas
p: Like Baal in Canaanite myth, Israel's God stills the roaring sea. But here the sea is no rival god.
b: In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle the storm god Baal defeats Yam (Sea) and becomes king. Israel's poets use the same imagery: God stills the raging sea (89:9; 93:3–4; 107:29). The psalm sets the uproar of the seas beside "the uproar of the peoples": the nations are as wild as the sea, and God calms both. The Gospels tell how Jesus calmed the sea with a word, and the disciples ask, "Who is this?" (Mark 4:39–41).

a: You make the lands where morning and evening go out shout for joy.
t: Where morning and evening go out
p: The 'goings-out' of morning and evening are the far east and far west: the whole world.
b: Motsa'e voqer va'erev are the places from which morning and evening "go out", the sunrise and sunset horizons. The phrase means the whole earth from east to west, as in 113:3 ("from the rising of the sun to where it goes down"). Some take it in time instead: every morning and evening rings with joy.

a: God's channel is full of water.
p: God's heavenly water supply, overflowing as rain.
b: Peleg elohim is "the channel (or stream) of God". Israel had no great rivers for irrigation like Egypt and Babylon and depended on rain (Deuteronomy 11:10–12). The picture is of a heavenly stream from which God waters the land, like the waters above the sky in Genesis 1:7, or the river that makes glad the city of God in 46:4. The Greek has "the river of God is filled with waters".

a: You have crowned the year of your goodness
p: Psalm 65 may have been sung at a harvest festival, when the year's crops came in.
b: 65:9–13 is a picture of the farming year: autumn rain softens the ground, furrows are plowed, grain sprouts, pastures green, flocks multiply. "You have crowned the year" may mean that the harvest is the year's crown. Many scholars connect the psalm with the Feast of Booths in autumn, when the harvest was finished and prayers for rain began, or with the spring barley harvest. The Mishnah's later prayers for rain at Booths (Taanit 1:1) show the link between the festival and the rains.

a: and your cart tracks drip with fat
p: Ma'gal is a cart track. God drives across the land like a farmer's wagon spilling abundance.
b: Ma'galekha, "your tracks", are the ruts left by a cart. God is pictured driving his chariot or harvest wagon across the land, and wherever the wheels go, richness drips out (deshen, "fat", the same word as 63:5). Some see the rain clouds as God's chariot (104:3).

a: They shout for joy; yes, they sing.
p: Creation itself joins the praise that began in Zion's silence.
b: The psalm begins with silence in Zion (65:1) and ends with meadows and valleys shouting and singing. The fields are dressed in flocks and grain like festival clothes. Creation's praise is a theme of 96:11–12, 98:7–8 and Isaiah 55:12 ("the mountains and the hills will break into song", a fresh rendering).

a: A song. A psalm.
p: 'We' in 66:1–12, 'I' in 66:13–20. A king, a leader, or any worshiper paying vows?
b: Psalm 66 has no author named in the Hebrew title. The first part calls all the earth to praise and speaks as "we", remembering the exodus and a time of testing. The second part is "I", paying vows with lavish sacrifices. The rich offerings in 66:15 suggest a king or leader speaking for the people; others think any worshiper made the people's story his own. Some connect the psalm with a national rescue such as Jerusalem's deliverance from Assyria in 701 BC (2 Kings 19:35–36). The Greek title adds "of resurrection", which led Christians to sing it at Easter.

a: that your enemies pretend to obey you
p: Kichesh means to deny, to deceive, and so to fawn or feign submission.
b: Yekhachashu lekha: kichesh means to lie or deny, and with "to" a superior it means to come cringing in false submission, the way defeated enemies flatter a conqueror they still hate (18:44; 81:15; Deuteronomy 33:29). The Greek has "your enemies will lie to you". God's power is so great that even his enemies must act loyal.

a: they crossed the river on foot.
p: The crossing of the Sea of Reeds and of the Jordan, remembered together.
b: The sea is the Sea of Reeds, where "the Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground" (Exodus 14:22). The river is probably the Jordan, which Israel crossed under Joshua "on dry ground" (Joshua 3:17). Psalm 114:3 pairs them in the same way. "There let us rejoice" pulls the present congregation into the past: the worshipers count themselves among those who crossed.

a: You have refined us the way silver is refined.
p: Suffering pictured as smelting: the fire burns away the waste and leaves pure silver.
b: Silver was refined by melting the ore and skimming off the dross (Proverbs 17:3; 25:4). The psalm reads Israel's hardships as testing, not as abandonment. The net, the crushing load, men riding over their heads, fire and water (66:11–12) are pictures of defeat, captivity and oppression. The prophets use the same image for God's purifying judgment (Isaiah 48:10; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3), and 1 Peter 1:6–7 applies it to Christian suffering.

a: You made men ride on our heads.
p: Probably conquerors driving chariots over the defeated, or making them bow so low they could be stepped on.
b: Ancient Assyrian and Egyptian reliefs show kings driving chariots over fallen enemies and setting their feet on the necks of captives (compare Joshua 10:24; Isaiah 51:23, "Bow down, so we may walk over you"). The picture is of total humiliation. "Fire and water" stand for every kind of danger (Isaiah 43:2: "when you walk through fire, you will not be burned").

a: but you brought us out to overflowing plenty
p: Revayah is 'saturation', the fullness of a well-watered field. The Greek has 'refreshment'.
b: Revayah is used in 23:5, "my cup overflows". The Greek has "into refreshment" (anapsychē), and some Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient versions may have read revachah, "relief, a wide place" (compare 18:19). Either way the movement is from crushing narrowness to open abundance.

a: I will make offerings of cattle with goats.
p: Burnt offerings of fattened animals, rams, cattle and goats: far more than an ordinary worshiper could bring.
b: A burnt offering (olah) was burned whole, so nothing was eaten. To offer fattened animals, rams, bulls and goats all together was lavish, the kind of sacrifice kings made at great occasions (1 Kings 8:62–64; 2 Chronicles 29:31–35). That is one reason many readers think the "I" of 66:13–20 is a king. The "smoke" (qetoret) of rams is the word often used for incense: the rising smoke of the sacrifice.

a: Come and listen, all you who fear God
p: Thanksgiving in Israel meant telling others what God had done.
b: A thanksgiving psalm is a testimony: the rescued person stands before the congregation and tells the story (22:22; 40:9–10; 116:14). "All you who fear God" may be the gathered worshipers, possibly including foreigners who worship Israel's God (compare 22:23; 115:11). The phrase was taken up in Acts for the God-fearing Gentiles (Acts 13:16, 26).

a: If I had looked with favor on evil in my heart
p: God would not hear someone who was holding on to evil. But he did hear.
b: The verse is a conditional: if I had cherished evil, God would not have listened (compare Isaiah 1:15; 59:2; Proverbs 15:29; John 9:31). The point is not that the singer is sinless, but that his prayer was honest. Because God did listen (66:19), the singer knows his heart was right with God. Many Christian traditions use this verse when they teach the confession of sin before prayer.
r: Isaiah 1:15; Isaiah 59:2; Proverbs 15:29; Proverbs 28:9; John 9:31; 1 John 3:21–22

a: May he make his face shine among us.
p: Psalm 67 opens with the words of the blessing of Aaron (Numbers 6:24–26), turned outward to the nations.
b: The opening echoes the priests' blessing: "May the LORD bless you and keep you. May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:24–25). The psalm changes "you" to "us" and the LORD to God (in the Elohistic style, see 56:10). Then it gives a new purpose: so that God's way will be known among all nations (67:2). Israel is blessed in order to be a blessing, as Abraham was (Genesis 12:2–3).

a: Let the peoples thank you, God.
p: Yodukha: let them acknowledge you, give you thanks, confess you.
b: Hodah means to acknowledge, to confess publicly, and so to thank or praise. It is the root of todah, the thank offering, and of the name Judah. The refrain in 67:3 and 67:5 asks that all the peoples confess and thank Israel's God. The psalm is arranged around its center (67:4), with the refrain on each side.

a: and you lead the nations on the earth
t: God as judge and shepherd of the nations
p: God judges the peoples fairly and leads the nations, as a shepherd leads a flock.
b: Tanchem, "you lead them", is the shepherd's word used in 23:3 and 78:72. The God of Israel is not only Israel's judge and guide; he rules and leads every nation. The center of the psalm, framed by its refrains, carries its main idea: the nations should rejoice because God's rule is just.

a: The land has given its crops.
p: A harvest is the sign of God's blessing, and the reason the ends of the earth will fear him.
b: The verb "has given" is past, but the next line, "will bless", is future. The psalm may have been sung at a harvest festival such as Weeks or Booths, giving thanks for a harvest just brought in and praying for blessing to come. The words echo Leviticus 26:4 ("The land will give its crops") and Ezekiel 34:27. In Jewish practice Psalm 67 is recited during the counting of the Omer between Passover and Weeks, often printed in the shape of the temple lampstand.

a: Let God rise up! Let his enemies scatter,
p: The psalm opens with Moses' words when the ark set out in the wilderness (Numbers 10:35).
b: "Each time the ark set out, Moses said, 'Rise up, LORD! Let your enemies scatter, let those who hate you run from your face'" (Numbers 10:35). Psalm 68 turns the prayer into the third person and puts "God" for "the LORD". Opening this way pictures God marching at the head of his people, as with the ark, from Sinai through the wilderness to his chosen mountain (68:7–8, 15–18, 24). Many think the psalm was sung when the ark was carried in procession into the temple.

a: Let God rise up!
p: Scholars agree Psalm 68 is the most difficult psalm to translate. Some think it is a collection of song openings.
b: Psalm 68 has more rare words and unclear lines than any other psalm; more than a dozen of its words appear nowhere else in the Bible. Readers have proposed many structures. W. F. Albright argued that it is a catalogue of the first lines of some thirty old poems. Most now read it as one hymn: a victory march of God from Sinai to Zion, with a procession into the sanctuary and a call to the nations. Its language has very old features, and many date parts of it to the time of the judges or the early kings. The notes here mark the uncertain places.

a: Build a highway for the one who rides through the desert plains.
t: Riding through the deserts, or on the clouds?
p: The Hebrew says 'deserts' ('aravot); many scholars read 'clouds', from a title of Baal. The Greek has 'the west'.
b: Larokhev ba'aravot is "for the rider in the 'aravot". In Hebrew 'aravot are dry plains, like the Arabah valley, and 68:7 speaks of God marching through the wasteland. But Ugaritic texts call Baal rkb 'rpt, "rider of the clouds", and 68:33 calls God "the rider through the highest heavens", so many think the poet took over Baal's title, perhaps with a letter changed, and claimed it for Israel's God. The Greek read 'erev, "evening", and has "who rides upon the west". Sollu may mean "build up a road" (as in Isaiah 40:3) or "lift up a song".

a: His name is Yah
p: Yah is a short form of the name YHWH, the one in Hallelujah.
b: Beyah shemo, "in Yah is his name" or "Yah is his name". Yah is the short form of the divine name, found in the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:2), in "Hallelujah" ("praise Yah") and in names like Elijah. The site usually renders the name "the LORD", but keeps "Yah" here because the verse is about the name itself. See 68:18, where Yah is rendered "the LORD".

a: God in his holy home is a father to orphans
p: The divine warrior is also the protector of orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners.
b: In the ancient Near East kings boasted that they protected orphans and widows (the Code of Hammurabi says so in its prologue and epilogue), and Israel's law made it a duty (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 10:18). Here God himself is father and judge for those without protection. The psalm joins God's power over kings (68:12, 14) with his care for the weakest, a pairing that recurs in 146:7–9 and in Mary's song (Luke 1:51–53).

a: He brings out prisoners into good times
p: Kosharot appears only here: 'prosperity', 'with singing', or 'with skill'. The Greek has 'with courage'.
b: The rare word kosharot may come from kasher, "to succeed, be right" (so "into prosperity"). Ugaritic texts mention the ktrt, goddesses of birth and song, so some translate "with singing". The Greek has "bound ones, with courage". God sets the lonely in a home and the prisoners free, which many hear as a memory of the exodus, when slaves became a household.

a: the earth shook, and the skies dripped
t: Psalm 68 and the Song of Deborah
p: 68:7–8 is almost the same as Judges 5:4–5, the oldest poem about God marching from the south.
b: Deborah's song says: "O LORD, as you came out of Seir, as you strode from the land of Edom, the earth quaked, the skies dripped ... at the LORD's presence, the One of Sinai, at the presence of the LORD, the God of Israel" (Judges 5:4–5). Psalm 68 has "God" where Judges has "the LORD", and the wasteland where Judges has Seir and Edom. Both speak of God coming from the southern desert, from Sinai, as in Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3. Psalm 68 also shares rare words with Judges 5: the "saddlebags" (68:13; Judges 5:16) and leading captives (68:18; Judges 5:12).

a: at the presence of God, the One of Sinai
p: Zeh sinai: 'this one of Sinai', an old title of God, 'the One of Sinai'.
b: Zeh sinai literally means "this Sinai". In very old Hebrew zeh could mean "the one of", like Arabic dhu, so the phrase is a title: "the One of Sinai". The site renders it the same way in Judges 5:5. Older translations took it as "even Sinai itself was moved" (KJV).

a: You poured out a generous rain, God.
p: Geshem nedavot, 'a rain of free gifts': generous, freely given rain on the weary land.
b: Nedavah is a freewill offering, a gift given without obligation. A "rain of free gifts" is generous rain, given freely. God's "inheritance" is his land, or his people (both are called so). Some think of the wilderness manna and quail, rained down from heaven (78:24–27); others of the rains that revived Canaan when Israel settled there.

a: Your living flock settled in it.
p: Chayyatekha is 'your living things', usually 'animals'. Here it means God's people, his flock or band.
b: Chayyah is a living creature, often a wild animal. 2 Samuel 23:11 and 23:13 use it for a band of soldiers. Here "your chayyah" is probably God's people pictured as his flock, which settled in the land he had prepared. The poor ('ani) of the next line may be all Israel, poor and weak until God provided.

a: The women who bring the news are a great army:
t: The women who bring the good news
p: The word for messengers is feminine: women spread the news of victory.
b: Hamevasserot is a feminine plural: "the women who bring good news". In Israel women sang to welcome the victors home (Exodus 15:20–21; 1 Samuel 18:6–7), and Isaiah 40:9 calls Zion herself a woman bringing good news. The Greek used euangelizomenois, the verb behind the New Testament's "gospel". The Prayer Book version, "great was the company of the preachers", made the messengers men; it became a chorus in Handel's Messiah, sung of the apostles preaching.

a: Even if you lie down between the saddlebags
p: The same rare word as Judges 5:16, where Reuben stays home 'between the saddlebags'.
b: Mishpetayim is rare; it may be saddlebags, sheepfolds or campfire stones. In Judges 5:16 Reuben stays "sitting between the saddlebags" while others fight. Here the line may rebuke those who stay home, or describe the women at home dividing rich plunder: a dove whose wings shine with silver and gold, perhaps a captured treasure or a woman's jewelry. The dove may be Israel (74:19; Hosea 7:11). Nobody is sure, and the verse is among the hardest in the Bible.

a: it snowed on Zalmon
p: Zalmon may be a dark mountain near Shechem (Judges 9:48) or in Bashan. Fleeing kings or bones are likened to snow.
b: Mount Zalmon ("dark one") appears in Judges 9:48 near Shechem, but here it may be a peak of Bashan, east of the Jordan, which is named next. The picture may be scattered weapons and bodies lying white like snow on a dark mountain, or kings fleeing like snowflakes in a storm. Some think of a real snowstorm during a battle, like the hail at Beth-horon (Joshua 10:11).

a: Mountain of God, mountain of Bashan!
p: Mount Hermon or the Golan peaks of Bashan look down in envy on little Zion.
b: Bashan, north-east of the Sea of Galilee, had high volcanic peaks and Mount Hermon (over 9,000 feet) at its northern edge. "Mountain of God" may be a way of saying "mighty mountain" (36:6 uses "mountains of God" in this sense), or it may admit that Hermon was a sacred mountain for the Canaanites. Yet God chose low Mount Zion (68:16). Bashan was also the land of King Og (Deuteronomy 3:1–11) and is the place from which God says he will bring back his enemies (68:22).

a: at the mountain God wanted for his home
p: God chooses the small hill of Zion over grander mountains, as he chose David over his brothers.
b: Mount Zion is only about 2,500 feet high, lower than the hills around it. Psalm 68 makes the contrast a point of theology: God's choice, not size, makes a mountain holy (78:68–69; 132:13–14). The Talmud (Megillah 29a) applies the verse to Sinai instead: when the high mountains each claimed the honor of the giving of the Torah, God chose humble Sinai, and these peaks were "blemished" by their pride.

a: Sinai is in the holy place.
p: God has brought Sinai with him: his presence that once filled the mountain now fills Zion.
b: The line is short and hard: Adonai vam sinai baqodesh, "the Lord among them, Sinai in holiness". Read as it stands, it means that the presence of Sinai has come to the holy place on Zion: Zion is the new Sinai. Many scholars change one letter to read "the Lord came from Sinai into the holy place" (see the variant), which fits Deuteronomy 33:2 ("The LORD came from Sinai"). The chariots in their thousands are the heavenly army (2 Kings 6:17; Deuteronomy 33:2).

a: You went up on high; you led captives away.
p: In the psalm God climbs Zion in triumph. Jewish tradition heard Moses on Sinai; Paul heard Christ's ascension.
b: In the psalm the victorious God ascends his mountain after battle, leading captives and receiving tribute, as a king did after a victory (Judges 5:12). Three readings grew from the verse. The Targum and the Talmud (Shabbat 88b–89a) apply it to Moses, who "went up" Sinai and "took" the Torah as a gift for human beings. Paul quotes it in Ephesians 4:8: "Going up on high, he led captivity captive, and he gave gifts to people" (a fresh rendering), and applies it to Christ, who rose and gave gifts to his church. Paul's "gave" agrees with the Targum and the Syriac against the Hebrew "took". See the variant and the chapter page.

a: he carries the load for us
p: Ya'amos: 'he carries a load'. God bears his people's burden, or carries them.
b: Ya'amos lanu can mean "he bears (our burden) for us" or "he carries us". Isaiah 46:3–4 uses the same verb for God carrying Israel from birth to old age, in contrast to idols that must be carried. The KJV's "daily loadeth us with benefits" adds words the Hebrew does not have.

a: belong the ways out from death
p: Totsa'ot lammavet: 'the ways out to death'. God controls the exits from death, or the exits into it.
b: Totsa'ot are "goings out" or exits. Most read the phrase as God holding the ways of escape from death. It could also mean that God has the power to send people out to death, which suits the next verse about his enemies. Christian readers heard in it the resurrection, and in Revelation 1:18 Christ says, "I hold the keys of death and of Hades".

a: From Bashan I will bring back.
t: Brought back from Bashan and the sea
p: God will bring back his enemies from wherever they hide, or bring back his people from far away.
b: God says he will bring back "from Bashan" and "from the deep places of the sea" but does not say whom. The next verse, about blood and dogs, suggests enemies: no hiding place, mountain or sea, will save them (compare Amos 9:2–3). Jewish tradition and the KJV ("I will bring my people again") read it as God bringing Israel home from exile, and the Talmud (Gittin 57b) applies the line to Jewish children drowned at sea in Roman times who will be raised.

a: so that your foot may stamp in blood
p: Like 58:10, this is the language of the battlefield: total defeat of the enemy.
b: The Hebrew "crush" (timchats) may be a slip for "bathe" (tirchats), which the Greek translated "be dipped" (see the variant). Either way the picture is of a victor walking through the blood of his enemies, with dogs licking it, as dogs licked Ahab's blood (1 Kings 22:38). It is a war song's picture, not a rule for behavior, and Christians often read it, as Augustine did, as the defeat of evil itself.

a: They have seen your processions, God
p: 68:24–27 describes a procession into the sanctuary: singers, musicians, girls with tambourines, tribal leaders.
b: The order of the procession is given: singers first, string players last, and between them young women beating hand drums (tof), like Miriam (Exodus 15:20). Leaders of four tribes walk behind: Benjamin and Judah from the south, Zebulun and Naphtali from the north. The procession may have carried the ark up to Zion, as when David brought it to Jerusalem with music and dancing (2 Samuel 6:5, 12–15), or been a regular festival march. Psalms 24 and 132 may belong to similar occasions.

a: the LORD, you who come from Israel's spring
p: Israel's 'spring' or 'fountain' may be its ancestor Jacob, or the source of its life.
b: Mimmeqor yisra'el is "from the spring of Israel". The image may be of descent: you who flow from Israel (Jacob) like water from a spring (compare Isaiah 48:1, "who came out of the waters of Judah", and Deuteronomy 33:28). Or it may mean God, "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13), as the source to bless.

a: There is little Benjamin, leading them
p: Benjamin, the youngest son and smallest tribe, heads the march. Saul, Israel's first king, was a Benjaminite.
b: Benjamin was Jacob's youngest son (Genesis 35:18) and the smallest tribe (1 Samuel 9:21). Its place at the front may recall Saul, the first king, or the fact that Jerusalem lay on Benjamin's border (Joshua 18:16). Rodem, "leading them", is uncertain; some read "ruling them". The leaders of Judah come "in their crowd" (rigmatam, a rare word, perhaps "their throng" or "their heap of stones"). The four tribes may stand for all Israel, south and north.

a: From your temple above Jerusalem
p: 'Above Jerusalem' may describe the temple on its height, or God's heavenly temple over the city.
b: Mehekhalekha 'al yerushalayim: "from your temple over Jerusalem". The phrase may also be read "because of your temple", taking min as giving the reason, or it may close the previous line ("you who have acted for us from your temple"), as some scholars divide it. The temple stood on the highest point of the city, north of David's town. Some read a heavenly temple above the earthly city. Either way the verse foresees foreign kings bringing tribute to God in Jerusalem, as Solomon received gifts (1 Kings 10:24–25), and as 72:10 and Isaiah 60:5–7 imagine on a world scale.

a: Rebuke the wild beast of the reeds
p: Probably Egypt, pictured as the crocodile or hippopotamus of the Nile marshes.
b: The "beast of the reeds" is most likely Egypt, whose Nile marshes held crocodiles and hippos and whose kings were pictured as river monsters (Ezekiel 29:3). The "herd of bulls among the calves of the peoples" may be the leaders of other nations. "Trampling on pieces of silver" may describe tribute-bearers bowing low, or nations greedy for silver. The Greek has "those who have been tested with silver". The next verse names Egypt and Cush (68:31), which supports the Egypt reading.

a: Cush will run to stretch out its hands to God.
p: Cush, the land south of Egypt in what is now Sudan, will reach out its hands in prayer or tribute.
b: Cush (the Greek and KJV "Ethiopia") was the kingdom on the Nile south of Egypt, now northern Sudan; it is not modern Ethiopia, though Ethiopian Christians have long read this verse as a promise for their land. Stretching out the hands is the posture of prayer (63:4) or of offering a gift. The verse inspired the Ethiopian church, the African American "Ethiopianism" movement of the 1800s, and many missionary hymns. Acts 8:26–39 tells how an official of the Cushite queen read Isaiah and was baptized.

a: to the rider through the highest heavens of long ago
p: God rides through the 'heavens of heavens of ancient time': the highest sky, as old as creation.
b: Shemei shemei qedem: "heavens of heavens of long ago". "Heavens of heavens" is a Hebrew way of saying the highest heavens (Deuteronomy 10:14; 1 Kings 8:27). Qedem can mean "ancient" or "east". The God who rides the clouds (compare 68:4) thunders, and his voice is strength, as in Psalm 29.

a: You are fearsome, God, from your holy places.
p: Sung at Pentecost in Jewish and Christian tradition, at Easter in the East, and as the Huguenots' battle psalm.
b: Because of Sinai (68:8, 17) and the gift of the law (68:18 in the Targum), many Jewish communities read Psalm 68 as the psalm of the day at Shavuot (Weeks), the festival of the giving of the Torah. Christians, reading 68:18 with Ephesians 4:8, used it for the Ascension and Pentecost. The Orthodox church sings 68:1–3 as the verses of the Easter (Pascha) hymn "Christ is risen from the dead". The French Protestants sang it to the Genevan tune "Que Dieu se montre seulement" as their "psalm of battles" in the wars of religion.

a: On "Lilies."
p: Shoshannim, 'lilies', heads Psalms 45, 69 and 80. Probably a tune; Jewish tradition heard Israel among thorns.
