b: 'Al shoshannim, "on lilies", may name a tune, an instrument shaped like a lily, or a kind of song. Jewish interpreters connected it with Song of Songs 2:2, "like a lily among thorns", and heard in these psalms the voice of Israel suffering among the nations. The Greek translated it "for those who will be changed".

a: for the water has reached my throat
p: Nefesh, often 'soul', here has its oldest sense: the throat, the neck, the breath.
b: The Hebrew says the waters have come "up to the nefesh". Nefesh is usually rendered "soul" or "life", but its root sense is the throat, the place of breathing and swallowing (Isaiah 5:14; Jonah 2:5). The singer is about to go under. The KJV's "waters are come in unto my soul" keeps the word but loses the picture. The image of drowning in deep water, mud and flood runs through 69:1–3 and 69:14–15 and links the psalm with Jonah 2.

a: I have sunk in the mud of the deep
p: Deep water and bottomless mud are pictures of death and Sheol, and of overwhelming trouble.
b: In Hebrew poetry the deep waters and the pit are the edge of the world of the dead (18:4–5; 88:6–7; Jonah 2:2–6). Jeremiah was lowered into a cistern where "there was no water, only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud" (Jeremiah 38:6, a fresh rendering; Jeremiah is not yet on this site). Many think the singer is gravely ill or under threat of death. The image returns in 69:14–15, where he asks to be pulled out.

a: Those who hate me without a cause
p: Jesus quotes this line, or the same words in 35:19, as fulfilled in him (John 15:25).
b: In John 15:25 Jesus says the world's hatred fulfills "the word written in their law: 'They hated me for no reason'" (a fresh rendering). The same Hebrew, son'ai chinnam, appears in 35:19 and in 109:3 in a similar form, and John's "law" here means the Scriptures in general. Because John also quotes 69:9 (John 2:17) and alludes to 69:21 (John 19:28–29), most think he has Psalm 69 in mind. It is one of the psalms the New Testament quotes most. The Plain renders the shared Hebrew as in 35:19.

a: what I never stole?
p: The singer is falsely accused of theft and made to pay damages for what he did not take.
b: Under Israel's law a thief repaid double or more (Exodus 22:1–4). The singer is treated as a thief and forced to "pay back" (ashiv) goods he never took. It may be literal, a court case lost to false witnesses, or a proverb for any unjust punishment. The line shows the psalm's setting: a man condemned by his community, not only attacked by enemies.

a: God, you know my foolishness.
p: The singer admits faults before God while insisting the hatred is undeserved.
b: The confession sits between two claims of innocence (69:4, 69:7). The singer does not say he is perfect: God knows his folly and his guilt. But in this conflict he suffers "for your sake" (69:7). Christian readers who heard Christ speaking in this psalm found this verse hard, since Christ had no sin (Hebrews 4:15). Augustine answered that Christ speaks here for his body, the church, taking its sins as his own (compare 2 Corinthians 5:21); others say the psalm points to Christ without every verse applying to him.

a: For I have carried insults for your sake
p: The singer suffers because of his loyalty to God: this is what made the psalm so important to the first Christians.
b: The insults come "for your sake" ('alekha): because the singer is God's, his zeal for God's house (69:9) brings ridicule. Jeremiah used the same words: "know that for your sake I bear insult" (Jeremiah 15:15, a fresh rendering), and many scholars think Psalm 69 comes from a prophet like Jeremiah or from a faithful group after the exile who were mocked for their loyalty. Jesus' words "You are blessed when people insult you ... on account of me" (Matthew 5:11) belong to the same tradition.

a: My brothers treat me as an outsider
p: The sufferer is a stranger even to his own brothers. The Gospels note that Jesus' brothers did not believe in him.
b: To be cut off by one's family was a deep shame in a society built on kinship (compare Job 19:13–19). Christian readers connected the verse with John 7:5, "not even his brothers were putting their faith in him", and Mark 3:21, where his family thought he was out of his mind. "My mother's sons" means full brothers, the closest kin.

a: Zeal for your house has eaten me up
p: John 2:17 quotes this when Jesus drives the traders from the temple; Romans 15:3 quotes the second line.
b: After Jesus overturns the money-changers' tables, "His disciples remembered the words in Scripture, 'Zeal for your house will eat me up'" (John 2:17). John changes the verb to the future, perhaps pointing to Jesus' death: his zeal for the temple will consume him. The second line, "the insults of those who insult you", is quoted in Romans 15:3: "For even Christ did not please himself; as it is written, 'The insults of those who insult you fell on me'" (a fresh rendering). The singer's zeal may have been for rebuilding the temple after the exile (compare Haggai 1:2–9) or for purity of worship.

a: I wept while my soul went without food
p: Mourning practices: weeping, fasting and sackcloth. Even his grief was mocked.
b: The Hebrew is literally "I wept with fasting of my soul". Some revocalize to "I humbled my soul with fasting" (compare 35:13), and the Greek has "I bent my soul in fasting". Fasting and sackcloth (69:11) were signs of mourning or repentance (2 Samuel 12:16; Joel 1:13). The singer mourned, perhaps over the temple or the nation, and was laughed at for it.

a: Those who sit at the gate talk about me
p: The city gate was the place of the elders, courts and public talk; the drinkers sang mocking songs.
b: The gate was where the elders sat and judged and where the town met (Ruth 4:1–2; Proverbs 31:23). To be talked about "at the gate" was to be the subject of public opinion and perhaps of legal charges. The "beer drinkers" (shekhar was beer or other strong drink) made him the subject of taunting songs, as Job complains (Job 30:9).

a: at a time you choose to show favor
p: Et ratson: an acceptable time, a time God has chosen to show goodwill.
b: 'Et ratson is "a time of favor", the moment when God is willing to accept. Isaiah 49:8 uses the phrase for the day of salvation: "In a time of favor I have answered you", and Paul quotes Isaiah in 2 Corinthians 6:2: "now is the day of salvation". Jewish tradition took 69:13 into the Sabbath afternoon prayer: "As for me, my prayer is to you, LORD, at a time of favor" is said before the Torah is read at Minchah, the afternoon service, since that hour was thought a time of grace.

a: or the pit shut its mouth on me
p: Be'er is a well or pit; here the mouth of the underworld closing over the singer.
b: Be'er is a well or cistern, and the pit is a picture of the grave (55:23). Once the stone was rolled over the opening, there was no way out. Sheol is pictured with a mouth that swallows the living (Numbers 16:30–33; Isaiah 5:14). The prayer is to be pulled out before it closes.

a: Come close to my soul and redeem it.
p: Ga'al and padah: to buy back as a family redeemer, and to pay a ransom.
b: Go'alah is from ga'al, the act of the family redeemer who buys back a relative's land or freedom (Leviticus 25:25–49; Ruth 4). Peded, "set free", is from padah, "ransom, pay to release". God is asked to act as the family member who comes to the rescue, "because of my enemies": their triumph would shame God's name.

a: and comforters, but I found not one.
p: The sufferer looks for sympathy and finds none, as in Lamentations and in the Gospels' passion.
b: "There is no one to comfort her" is the refrain of Lamentations 1 (1:2, 9, 16, 17, 21). The friends who came to comfort Job became accusers (Job 16:2). Christian tradition heard this verse in Gethsemane, where the disciples slept (Mark 14:37–41), and at the cross, when all fled (Mark 14:50). In the Latin of 69:20–21, Improperium exspectavit cor meum, it is the offertory chant of Palm Sunday in the Roman rite.
r: Lamentations 1:2; Lamentations 1:16; Job 16:2; Isaiah 63:5; Mark 14:37–41; Mark 14:50

a: They put poison in my food
p: Rosh is a bitter, poisonous plant. The Greek has 'gall', the word in Matthew 27:34.
b: Rosh is a bitter plant, perhaps poison hemlock or a poppy, and stands for poison in general (Deuteronomy 29:18; 32:32–33). The Greek has cholē, "gall, bile". Instead of food, the singer is given poison; instead of water, chomets, vinegar or sour wine. A mourner was usually given food by friends (2 Samuel 3:35; Jeremiah 16:7); here the meal of comfort becomes cruelty.

a: and when I was thirsty they made me drink vinegar
t: Gall and vinegar at the cross
p: All four Gospels tell of sour wine offered to Jesus on the cross, and Matthew adds gall.
b: Matthew says the soldiers "gave him wine mixed with gall to drink. He tasted it and would not drink" (Matthew 27:34), and later someone filled a sponge "with vinegar" for him (Matthew 27:48; Mark 15:36; Luke 23:36). John says Jesus, "so that the Scripture would be fulfilled", said "I am thirsty", and they lifted to his mouth a sponge full of sour wine (John 19:28–29, a fresh rendering). Sour wine (oxos) was the cheap drink of soldiers, so the offer may have been kind or cruel. The Gospel writers saw the whole scene as the psalm come true.
r: Matthew 27:34; Matthew 27:48; Mark 15:23; Mark 15:36; Luke 23:36; John 19:28–30

a: Let their table in front of them become a trap
p: 69:22–28 is one of the longest curses in the Psalms. Romans 11:9–10 quotes it of Israel's unbelief.
b: Seven curses follow: a trapped table, darkened eyes, shaking hips, poured-out wrath, a ruined camp, guilt added to guilt, and names erased from the scroll of life. Their table, the place of feasting and friendship, should become their snare. Paul quotes 69:22–23 from the Greek in Romans 11:9–10: "Let their table become a snare and a trap and a stumbling block and a payback for them; let their eyes be darkened so they do not see, and bend their backs forever" (a fresh rendering). He applies it to the part of Israel that did not believe, but goes on at once to say their stumbling is not final (Romans 11:11–12, 25–26). See the chapter page on how Jews and Christians have prayed this passage.

a: and make their hips shake all the time
p: Shaking loins is the posture of terror and weakness; the Greek has 'bend their back'.
b: The motnayim are the hips or waist, where strength was thought to sit (Nahum 2:10). Shaking hips are a sign of terror (Isaiah 21:3; Daniel 5:6). The Greek has "bend their back always", the picture of a slave or prisoner bowed under a load, and Paul follows the Greek (Romans 11:10).

a: Pour out your fury on them.
p: The image of God's anger poured out like liquid appears in the prophets and in Revelation's bowls.
b: Shefokh 'alehem za'mekha: pour out your fury. Wrath is poured like water or molten metal (79:6; Jeremiah 10:25; Ezekiel 22:22). The last book of the Bible uses the same picture: "Go and pour out the seven bowls of God's anger on the earth" (Revelation 16:1). Psalm 79:6, after Jerusalem's fall, asks God to pour out his anger on the nations who do not know him.

a: Let their encampment be a ruin
p: Peter quotes this in Acts 1:20 of Judas, changing 'their' to 'his'.
b: Before choosing a replacement for Judas, Peter says, "It is written in the book of Psalms, 'Let his homestead become desolate, and let there be no one living in it', and, 'Let another take his position'" (Acts 1:20, a fresh rendering). The first line is this verse, made singular; the second is 109:8. A tirah is a nomad's walled camp or settlement (Genesis 25:16). For the early church, the curses on the betrayer of the righteous sufferer had come true in the betrayer of Jesus.

a: For they hunt down the one you have struck
t: Kicking a man when he is down
p: The enemies attack someone God has already struck: perhaps a sick man, suffering under God's hand.
b: The singer sees his suffering as coming in some sense from God ("the one you have struck"), and the enemies take it as proof that he is guilty, as Job's friends did. Instead of pity they pile on. Isaiah 53:4 has the same picture: "we thought of him as struck, hit by God and afflicted" (a fresh rendering). The Greek has "they added to the pain of my wounds" (see the variant).

a: Let them be wiped out of the scroll of life
t: Wiped out of the scroll of life
p: The 'scroll of life' is God's register of the living. Later it became the book of eternal life.
b: Sefer chayyim is literally "the scroll of living ones": God's register of those alive, like a city's roll of citizens (Isaiah 4:3; Ezekiel 13:9). To be wiped out of it was to die (Exodus 32:32–33). In later Jewish and Christian writings it became the book of those who will live forever (Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; 20:12–15). The risen Christ promises, "I will never erase that person's name from the book of life" (Revelation 3:5). The Jewish High Holy Day prayers ask to be written in the book of life.
r: Exodus 32:32–33; Isaiah 4:3; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 20:12–15; 56:8

a: With a song I will praise God's name
p: Abruptly the psalm turns from lament and curse to praise and a vow of thanks.
b: As in many laments (22:22; 28:6; 31:21), the cry for help turns into thanks. Some think an answer from God came between 69:29 and 69:30, perhaps through a priest. Others think the singer praises in advance, in faith that he will be heard. The turn shows that the curses are not the psalm's last word.

a: The LORD will like that better than an ox
p: A song of thanks pleases God more than a bull. Not a rejection of sacrifice but a ranking.
b: Several psalms rank praise and obedience above animal sacrifice (40:6; 50:13–14; 51:16–17), as Samuel did (1 Samuel 15:22) and the prophets after him (Hosea 6:6). "With horns and hooves" means a full-grown, ritually fit bull (Leviticus 11:3). After the temple fell in AD 70, Jewish teachers used such verses to show that prayer could take the place of sacrifice (compare Hosea 14:2). Hebrews 13:15 calls praise "a sacrifice of praise", "the fruit of lips".

a: and does not despise his prisoners
p: Captives: perhaps literal prisoners, or the exiles, or all who are bound by trouble.
b: "His prisoners" (asirav) may be literal prisoners, the people of Judah in exile, or anyone held captive by suffering (compare 68:6; 102:20; 107:10). The closing verses (69:34–36) widen the psalm from one person to Zion and the towns of Judah, which suggests that the psalm was used, and perhaps shaped, among the exiles or the community that returned.

a: and build the towns of Judah again
p: The ending looks forward to Zion saved and Judah's towns rebuilt: a hope of the exile.
b: "Build again" and "live there and own it" fit the time when Judah lay in ruins after 587 BC and its people hoped to return (Isaiah 44:26; Jeremiah 33:10–11; Ezekiel 36:10). Some scholars think the verses were added to David's psalm for use in that time; others think David himself looks ahead. Either way the personal lament ends in hope for the whole people, and "those who love his name" inherit the land.

a: To bring to remembrance.
p: Lehazkir also heads Psalm 38. It may refer to the 'memorial' offering, or simply to reminding God.
b: Lehazkir, "to cause to remember", stands in the titles of Psalms 38 and 70. It may mean the psalm was sung when the azkarah, the "token portion" of the grain offering, was burned (Leviticus 2:2; 24:7), or that it was meant to "remind" God of the one praying. The Greek has "for remembrance, that the Lord may save me", joining the title to the first words of the psalm. The Targum links it with the incense offering.

a: God, to rescue me!
p: Psalm 70 repeats the end of Psalm 40 with small changes, most of them in the names for God.
b: Psalm 70 is almost the same as 40:13–17, and the Plain uses the wording of 40:13–17 wherever the Hebrew is the same. The Hebrew differs in these places: 70:1 lacks the opening verb "may it please you" (retseh) and has "God" for the first "LORD"; 70:2 lacks "together" (yachad) and "to sweep it away" (lispotah); 70:3 has "turn back" (yashuvu) for "be stunned" (yashommu) and lacks "to me"; 70:4 has "God" for "the LORD"; 70:5 has "God, hurry to me" (chushah li) for "may the Lord keep me in mind" (yachashov li), and "LORD" for "my God". Several of the changes put "God" for "the LORD", the habit of the Elohistic Psalter (see 56:10), though "LORD" stays twice.

a: hurry to my help!
p: The opening of Psalm 70 became the first words of the church's daily prayer.
b: From the 400s, monks began each prayer hour with 70:1: in Latin, Deus, in adiutorium meum intende; Domine, ad adiuvandum me festina, "God, come to my help; Lord, hurry to help me." John Cassian (Conferences 10.10) recommended it as a prayer to repeat at all times, for every need. The Benedictine Rule fixed it at the start of the hours, and it still opens most of the hours in the Roman Liturgy of the Hours and in Anglican Evensong ("O God, make speed to save us").

a: those who say, "Aha! Aha!"
p: He'ach is a cry of gloating, a jeering laugh at someone's fall.
b: He'ach he'ach is a mocking shout of triumph, like "ha-ha!" (35:21, 25; Ezekiel 25:3; 26:2). The enemies enjoy the singer's trouble. The prayer that they "turn back because of their shame" (literally "on the heel" or "as the wages" of their shame) asks that their gloating bring their own disgrace.

a: I am poor and needy;
p: Ani ve'evyon: a common self-description in the psalms, of material poverty and of dependence on God.
b: 'Ani ve'evyon, "afflicted and needy", is how many psalm singers describe themselves (40:17; 86:1; 109:22). The words can mean literal poverty, but in the psalms they also describe anyone without power who must depend on God. Some scholars think "the poor" became almost a name for the faithful in Israel after the exile. The phrase leads into Psalm 71, which many manuscripts join to Psalm 70, and into Psalm 72, where the king saves "the needy" (72:12–13).

a: I take shelter in you, LORD;
p: Psalm 71 is the only psalm in Book II after Psalm 43 with no title. It may belong with Psalm 70.
b: Every psalm from 51 to 70 carries a title; Psalm 71 does not. Many medieval Hebrew manuscripts join it to Psalm 70, and the two share Hebrew phrases: le'ezrati chushah, hurry to my help (70:1; 71:12), yevoshu, let them be shamed (70:2; 71:13, 24), and mevaqshei ra'ati, those who seek my harm (70:2; 71:13, 24). The Greek gives it a title of its own: "Of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first ones taken captive", linking it with the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35) and the exile. In the Dead Sea Scroll 4QPs-a (copied in the second century BC) Psalm 71 comes right after Psalm 38, another sign that the order of the psalms was still fluid.

a: never let me end up in shame.
p: 71:1–3 is close to 31:1–3; other lines echo Psalms 22, 35, 38 and 40.
b: The opening repeats 31:1–3 with small changes, and the Plain uses the wording of 31:1–3 wherever the Hebrew is the same; and the psalm borrows widely: trust since the womb from 22:9–10, the pleas not to be far off and to hurry to help from 22:11, 22:19, 38:21–22 and 40:13, and the wish that those who seek the singer's harm be shamed from 35:4, 35:26 and 40:14. Scholars call this style anthological. The older singer prays in the words he has known all his life, which suits a psalm about trusting God "since I was young" (71:5, 17).

a: Be a rock to live in for me
t: A rock to live in, or a rock of refuge?
p: Ma'on is a dwelling; 31:2 has ma'oz, a stronghold. The two words differ by one letter.
b: The Leningrad Codex has tsur ma'on, "a rock of dwelling". Psalm 31:2 has tsur ma'oz, "a rock of shelter", and some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek ("a God protector and a strong place") read something like that here too. The letters nun and zayin are easily confused. See the variant. "You have given the order to save me" is also a change from 31:2, "a fortress house to save me", perhaps from a similar-looking word.

a: You are the one who cut me loose from my mother's body.
t: The one who cut me loose
p: Gozi is rare: 'the one who cut me' (like a cord), or 'my benefactor'. The Greek has 'my protector'.
b: Gozi may be from gazaz, "to cut, shear": God is like the midwife who cut the cord and brought the child out. Or it may be from an Aramaic word for "repay, reward". The Greek has "you are my protector". 22:9–10 says the same thing more plainly: "you are the one who pulled me out of the womb" (22:9). Trust that began at birth carries the singer into old age (71:9, 18).

a: I have become like a portent to many
p: Mofet is a portent, a sign: something people point to, either in wonder or as a warning.
b: A mofet is a wonder or a sign, often a warning of God's judgment (Deuteronomy 28:46; Ezekiel 12:6). The singer's troubles are so great that people see him as a lesson of what happens to those God abandons (compare 71:11). Others take it positively: his life has been a wonder of God's protection. Isaiah's children were "signs and portents in Israel" (Isaiah 8:18).

a: Do not throw me away in my old age.
p: Psalm 71 is the Bible's prayer of old age: the fear of being discarded when strength fails.
b: The singer has come "into old age and white hair" (71:18). His enemies say God has abandoned him (71:11), perhaps because his strength or fortune has failed. In a society that honored the old (Leviticus 19:32), the elderly could still be pushed aside, and the law had to protect parents (Exodus 21:17; Proverbs 23:22). The psalm has long been read at the bedside of the aged and the dying; Isaiah 46:4 gives God's answer: "even to your old age I am the same, and to gray hairs I will carry you" (a fresh rendering).

a: Let those who accuse me be put to shame
p: Sotenei nafshi: 'the accusers of my soul', from satan, to accuse or oppose.
b: Sotenei is from the verb satan, "to accuse, oppose", the root of the title "the Accuser" in Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3. Here it means human opponents who bring charges against the singer, perhaps in court, as in 109:4, 109:20 and 109:29. It does not refer to Satan.

a: though I do not know how to count them
p: Sefarot: 'numbers'. The Greek has 'I did not know letters' (literature).
b: Lo yada'ti sefarot: "I do not know numbers", that is, God's saving acts are too many to count (compare 40:5). The word can also mean "writings", and the Greek has "I have not known literature" (grammateias). Some church fathers took the Greek to mean that the singer was an unlearned man, saved not by learning but by God's grace, and Augustine discussed the line at length as a warning against pride in learning.

a: I will call to mind your righteousness, yours alone.
p: Tsedaqah is a key word of Psalm 71: God's righteousness is his faithfulness in rescuing.
b: Tsedaqah appears five times in Psalm 71 (71:2, 15, 16, 19, 24). It is not only fairness in judging but God's faithfulness to his commitments, which shows itself in rescue: "Because you are righteous, rescue me" (71:2). Paul builds on this sense when he speaks of "the righteousness of God" revealed in the gospel (Romans 1:17; 3:21–26).

a: until I make known your arm to a generation
t: Passing faith to the next generation
p: The old singer wants to live long enough to tell the next generation what God has done.
b: The prayer to be kept alive has a purpose: to tell "your arm" (zero'akha, God's strength in action, as in the exodus, Deuteronomy 4:34) to a generation not yet born. Handing on God's deeds from parents to children is a duty of Israel's faith (78:4–7; Deuteronomy 6:20–25; Joel 1:3) and of the church's (2 Timothy 2:2).

a: out of the deep places of the earth
p: Brought up from the 'depths of the earth': rescue from near death, or more?
b: The "deep places" (tehomot) of the earth are the underworld waters (Jonah 2:3–6). To be brought up from them is to be brought back from the edge of death (30:3; 86:13). The written text (Ketiv) says "us" and "give us life", the spoken reading (Qere) "me"; the Greek agrees with "me". Many Christian readers read the line as a hint of resurrection, though most scholars think the singer means recovery in this life.

a: Holy One of Israel
p: A title of God found 25 times in Isaiah and only three times in the Psalms (71:22; 78:41; 89:18).
b: Qedosh yisra'el is the favorite name for God in Isaiah (for example Isaiah 1:4; 6:3; 41:14). In the Psalms it appears only here, in 78:41 and in 89:18. Its presence is one reason some scholars think Psalm 71 is late, influenced by the Isaiah tradition; others think Isaiah drew it from the temple worship of Jerusalem.

a: I also will thank you on the harp
p: The nevel and the kinnor were the two main stringed instruments of the temple.
b: The nevel ("harp", sometimes "lute") and the kinnor ("lyre") were the stringed instruments of the Levite musicians (1 Chronicles 15:16; 25:1). The kinnor was the portable lyre David played for Saul (1 Samuel 16:23). An old man promising to play both is promising his best music. Compare 57:8.

a: Of Solomon.
p: Lishlomoh can mean 'by', 'for' or 'about' Solomon. The Greek has 'for Solomon'.
b: Only Psalms 72 and 127 carry Solomon's name. The Hebrew le can mean authorship ("by Solomon"), dedication ("for Solomon") or subject ("about Solomon"). The Greek has eis Salōmōn, "for Solomon". Because 72:20 calls the whole collection "the prayers of David", many Jewish and Christian readers have said that David prayed this psalm for his son at the end of his life (Rashi; the Midrash; compare 1 Kings 1:28–40), while others think Solomon wrote it about his own reign or for his heir. Critical scholars mostly see a coronation prayer for any king of David's line.

a: God, give your rulings to the king
t: A prayer for a just king
p: The psalm asks God to give the king his own justice, so that the king can give it to the poor.
b: The first verse is the key to the whole psalm. Justice (mishpat) and righteousness (tsedaqah) are God's to give; the king rules well only if he receives them. Solomon prayed for just this: "Give your servant a heart that listens, so he can judge your people" (1 Kings 3:9). Ancient Near Eastern kings made the same claim: Hammurabi said the gods made him king "to make justice appear in the land" (prologue of his laws). What is unusual in Israel is how much of the psalm is about the poor (72:2, 4, 12–14).
r: 1 Kings 3:9; 1 Kings 3:28; 2 Samuel 23:3–4; Isaiah 11:1–5; Jeremiah 23:5; Proverbs 16:12

a: your righteousness to the king's son
t: The king and the king's son
p: Parallel lines: 'the king' and 'the king's son' are probably one person, a king of royal birth.
b: In Hebrew poetry the second line often restates the first. "The king's son" is likely the same king, stressing that he is of David's line, the rightful heir (compare 2 Samuel 7:12–16). The Targum renders the verse, "God, give the knowledge of your laws to King Messiah, and your righteousness to the son of King David", the clearest sign of the Jewish messianic reading.

a: Let him judge your people in righteousness
p: The verbs can be read 'May he ...' (a prayer) or 'He will ...' (a promise). The KJV chose 'He shall'.
b: Most of the verbs in Psalm 72 are imperfect forms, which in Hebrew can be future ("he will judge") or wishes ("may he judge"). A few are clearly wishes (72:8, 72:15, 72:17). The KJV made the whole psalm a prophecy ("He shall judge"), which suited a messianic reading. Most modern versions make it a prayer. The site follows the prayer reading through 72:11 and the plain future in 72:12–14, where the Hebrew says "For he will rescue".

a: May the mountains carry peace to the people
p: Shalom is peace, wholeness and prosperity; the mountains and hills will bear it like a crop.
b: Shalom is far more than the absence of war: it is wholeness, health and prosperity. The mountains and hills, Israel's farmland, will "carry" it like a harvest (compare 72:16). Justice and fertility go together in the Bible's picture of a good king: when the king is just, the land flourishes (Leviticus 26:3–6; Isaiah 32:15–17).

a: and break the oppressor in pieces
p: No other royal text gives so much space to the poor. The king's power exists to protect them.
b: The poor, the needy and the oppressed appear in 72:2, 72:4, 72:12, 72:13 and 72:14. The king's first duty is to them, and his crushing of the oppressor is for their sake. Deuteronomy's law of the king (Deuteronomy 17:14–20) limits his wealth; Psalm 72 gives his purpose. Prophets judged kings by this standard: "He judged the cause of the poor and needy ... Is not that what it means to know me?" (Jeremiah 22:16, a fresh rendering).

a: May they fear you as long as the sun lasts
t: Fear you, or may he live long?
p: The Hebrew says 'they will fear you'; the Greek has 'he will remain with the sun'.
b: Suddenly the Hebrew addresses God ("you") in a psalm about the king. The Greek has "and he will continue as long as the sun", which reads a different verb (ya'arikh, "he will prolong") and keeps the focus on the king. Many modern versions follow the Greek. The site follows the Hebrew: the king's just rule leads people to fear God for all generations. See the variant.

a: May he come down like rain on mown grass
p: A good king refreshes his land like rain on a field after mowing. The Greek has 'on a fleece'.
b: After the first hay was cut, the field needed rain to grow again (Amos 7:1). The image recalls David's last words: a just ruler "is like morning light as the sun rises ... from the shine, from the rain, green grass comes up from the ground" (2 Samuel 23:4). Gez can also mean a fleece, and the Greek and Latin have "like rain on a fleece". Christian writers linked that with Gideon's fleece (Judges 6:36–40) and read it of the quiet coming of Christ into Mary's womb, an image used in Advent hymns.

a: Let the righteous bloom in his days
p: The Hebrew has 'the righteous'; some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek have 'righteousness'.
b: Tsaddiq, "the righteous one", may be the righteous people in general, flourishing under a just king. The Greek, the Syriac and some Hebrew manuscripts have tsedeq, "righteousness", which matches "peace" in the next line. The difference is a single letter. See the variant.

a: May he rule from sea to sea,
p: The ideal borders of David's kingdom, widened to the whole world. Zechariah 9:10 repeats the line of the coming king.
b: "The River" is the Euphrates (1 Kings 4:21, "Solomon was ruler over all the kingdoms from the River"). "From sea to sea" may mean from the Mediterranean to the Dead Sea or the Red Sea (Exodus 23:31), or simply from one end of the world to the other. Zechariah 9:9–10 uses the same words for the humble king riding a donkey, "his rule will be from sea to sea, from the River to the ends of the earth" (a fresh rendering), and Matthew 21:5 applies that king to Jesus. Canada's motto, A mari usque ad mare, comes from the Latin of this verse.
r: 1 Kings 4:21; 1 Kings 4:24; Exodus 23:31; Genesis 15:18; Zechariah 9:9–10; 2:8; Matthew 21:5

a: Before him may the desert peoples kneel
p: Tsiyyim are dwellers in dry places, desert nomads. The Greek has 'Ethiopians'.
b: Tsiyyim are those who live in the tsiyyah, the dry land: nomad tribes, or desert animals (Isaiah 13:21). Some scholars change the word to tsarim, "foes", to match the next line. The Greek has "Ethiopians", perhaps reading kushim. To "lick the dust" is to bow with the face to the ground, as captives did before a conqueror (Isaiah 49:23; Micah 7:17).

a: May the kings of Tarshish and the islands
t: Tarshish, the islands, Sheba and Seba
p: The far west and the far south: the ends of the known world bring tribute.
b: Tarshish was a distant port in the far west, probably in Spain or Sardinia, reached by large ships (Jonah 1:3; 1 Kings 10:22). The "islands" (iyyim) are the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean. Sheba was in south Arabia (modern Yemen), the home of the queen who visited Solomon (1 Kings 10:1–10). Seba may be in Africa, south of Egypt (Isaiah 43:3; 45:14). Together they mean the whole world, west and south.
r: 1 Kings 10:1–10; 1 Kings 10:22; Jonah 1:3; Isaiah 43:3; Isaiah 60:6–9; Genesis 10:7

a: May the kings of Sheba and of Seba
p: Christians read 72:10–11 with Isaiah 60:6 and Matthew 2:11: the Magi as the kings bringing gifts.
b: Matthew does not call the Magi kings. But Christian readers joined Matthew 2:11 ("they opened their treasure chests and brought out gifts for him: gold, frankincense and myrrh") with this psalm and with Isaiah 60:3–6 ("from Sheba they will come, bringing gold and frankincense", a fresh rendering), and by the time of Tertullian (about AD 200) the Magi were said to be "almost kings". Psalm 72 is the responsorial psalm for the feast of Epiphany in the Roman Catholic lectionary, and its verse "all kings will bow down to him" is sung at that feast in many churches.

a: For he will rescue the needy who cry for help
t: Why the king deserves the world
p: The nations bow to him because he rescues the needy. Power is given for the sake of the poor.
b: Ki, "for, because", ties 72:12–14 to the world rule of 72:8–11. The king receives the world's tribute because he hears the poor who cry out and have no other helper. It is the picture of God himself (68:5; 146:7–9), shared with a human king. The verses are a measure for any ruler, and the Jewish and Christian messianic readings both stress them.

a: and their blood will be precious in his eyes
p: The lives of the poor matter to him. He buys them back as a family redeemer would.
b: "He will buy back" is yig'al, the verb of the family redeemer (see 69:18). The king acts as next of kin to the poor. That their "blood" (life) is "precious" in his eyes means he will not let them be killed cheaply (compare 116:15, "precious in the eyes of the LORD is the death of his faithful ones", a fresh rendering; and 2 Kings 1:13–14).

a: May he live, and may Sheba's gold be given him.
p: The Hebrew has 'he will give him': the poor man may give gold to the king, or the king give to the poor.
b: The verbs are singular with no clear subject: "may he live, and he will give to him of the gold of Sheba, and he will pray for him always". Most translations make the king the one who lives and receives gold, and the people the ones who pray for him. Some Jewish interpreters (Rashi) took the rescued poor man as the one who lives and receives gold from the king, and blesses him in thanks. "May he live!" is the Hebrew of the acclamation "Long live the king!" (1 Samuel 10:24; 1 Kings 1:39).

a: May there be plenty of grain in the land
p: Pissat appears only here, 'abundance'; the KJV took it as 'a handful'.
b: Pissat bar is usually taken as "abundance of grain", from a root "to spread". The KJV's "an handful of corn" followed a Jewish tradition that took it as a small amount that grows into a harvest; Christian preachers then compared it to the mustard seed (Matthew 13:31–32). Grain waving even on the tops of the mountains, where nothing usually grows, is a picture of extraordinary plenty, like Amos 9:13.

a: May his name grow as long as the sun shines.
t: Yinnon: a name for the Messiah
p: The rare verb yinnon, 'may it sprout, grow', became in rabbinic tradition a name of the Messiah.
b: The verb yinnon (spoken reading; the written form is yanin) is from nin, "offspring": "may his name have offspring", that is, may it spread and continue. The Talmud reads lifne shemesh yinnon shemo as "before the sun, Yinnon is his name": one school of Rabbi Yannai said the Messiah's name is Yinnon (Sanhedrin 98b), and the Messiah's name is one of the seven things created before the world, proved from this verse (Pesachim 54a). The site's "as long as the sun shines" takes lifne as "while" the sun lasts.

a: May people bless themselves by him
p: The language echoes God's promise to Abraham that all nations will be blessed through him.
b: Veyitbarekhu vo, "let them bless themselves by him", uses the same form as Genesis 22:18: "all the nations of the earth will bless themselves by your offspring". To "bless oneself by" someone is to say "May I be like him!" when asking for a blessing. The king of David's line becomes the channel of Abraham's blessing to the nations. The Greek adds "all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him", which makes the echo of Genesis 12:3 and 28:14 even clearer. See the variant.

a: Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel
t: The doxology that ends Book II
p: 72:18–19 is not part of Psalm 72 but the closing praise of the second book of the Psalter.
b: Each of the five books of the Psalms ends with a doxology, a short formula of praise: 41:13, 72:18–19, 89:52, 106:48, and Psalm 150 as the close of all. This one is the fullest. It praises "the LORD God" (a rare use of the name YHWH in this Elohistic book) and ends, like 41:13 and 89:52, "Amen and amen." It was probably added by the editors who joined Psalms 42–72 to the first book. Some think the Psalter's five books were meant to mirror the five books of Moses (Midrash Tehillim 1:2).

a: May his glory fill all the earth.
t: The earth filled with his glory
p: The doxology ends with a hope found in Numbers 14:21, Isaiah 6:3 and Habakkuk 2:14.
b: God swears in Numbers 14:21, "as surely as the LORD's glory will fill all the earth". The seraphs sing in Isaiah 6:3 that "the whole earth is full of his glory", and Habakkuk 2:14 looks for the earth to be filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory "as the waters cover the sea". Placed after the prayer for a king whose rule reaches the ends of the earth (72:8), the doxology says that the goal of his rule is God's glory, not his own.

a: Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse.
p: A colophon, a scribe's closing note. Yet more psalms of David follow in Books III to V. Why?
b: This note marks the end of an earlier collection, probably Psalms 3–72 or 51–72, called "the prayers of David". The editors who added Psalms 73–150 kept it, though eighteen later psalms are also called "of David" (for example 86, 101, 103, 108–110, 138–145). Gerald Wilson argued that the note, together with the royal psalms placed at the seams of the books (2, 72, 89), shows that the Psalter tells a story: the Davidic kingdom is founded (Book I), passed on to Solomon (Psalm 72), and seen to fail (Psalm 89), before Books IV–V turn to the LORD as king. The Greek has "the hymns of David son of Jesse are ended".

a: David son of Jesse
p: The Psalter recalls David's humble origins, as his own last words do.
b: "David son of Jesse" is how Saul's men spoke of him with contempt (1 Samuel 20:27; 22:7) and how David's last words begin: "The declaration of David son of Jesse" (2 Samuel 23:1). Isaiah 11:1 foresees "a shoot from the stump of Jesse", a new king from David's root. The colophon thus ends Book II on David's family line, the line Psalm 72 prays for.
